title: A Borrowed Hand
html:
The crocodile does not move. Kyle has been watching it for four minutes — the NeoCortex timestamps involuntarily, a facility habit he never unlearned — and the animal has not moved once, its jaw resting on the heat rock with the particular stillness of something that has learned patience as a survival strategy. He understands that. The tank glass is clean. Someone wipes it daily. That detail costs more than the crocodile.

*The smell is chum and bleach and something underneath both that he is choosing not to identify.*

Hua's hands are the first thing he catalogued when they brought him in, before the chair, before the table, before the long lacquered surface where Silence lay with its friction sheath unbuckled and set beside it like a deed already filed. Real skin. Real nails, cut short and unpainted. The NeoCortex flagged them the same way it flags fire exits and secondary egress points — as a structural anomaly in an environment where chrome is the baseline. In the Gray Zone, unaugmented hands mean poverty or principle. In this room, at this table, they mean neither. They mean she does not need to be faster than anyone in the room, because everyone in the room is afraid of her, which is the only speed that matters.

*His hands are the same category of object for a completely different reason, and she does not know that yet, and he is not going to tell her.*

She stops pacing in front of the tank. The two men at his shoulders have not moved in ninety seconds. The toolkit on the floor between them is a black nylon roll, the kind that fastens with two snaps and opens flat, and Kyle has not looked directly at it because looking at it is information he is not yet prepared to have. Silence is on the table. The angle Hua arranged it — parallel to the table edge, saya toward her, handle toward the room's center — is the arrangement of something already appraised. She has not touched the blade. She has touched the saya twice, with two fingers, the way you confirm a purchase without appearing to need it. Across the table, the chum barrel stands beside the tank, its lid set aside with the same ritual neatness as the friction sheath. The room smells like an argument that was settled before Kyle arrived.

"The Vásquez shipment," Hua says. Not a question. She does not raise her voice. "The Syndicate's contracted route. The Syndicate's contracted fee." She turns from the tank and looks at him with the expression of someone who has already finished a meal and is now simply clearing the table. "You took both."

He says nothing. The NeoCortex is at thirty-one percent and still burning cycles on the exits — service hatch behind the tank, single door behind him, ventilation width insufficient — and on Hua's hands, and on the crocodile, which has still not moved. His jaw aches where the left molar meets the chrome bracket they installed at the facility, the one that never sat right, and the ache has a specific frequency that tells him the takedown involved something harder than a fist.

"The punishment," Hua says, and she picks up Silence by the saya — not the handle, the saya, careful, informed — "for theft from the Syndicate's contracted work is the hand that took it."

*He has been refusing that upgrade for eight years. He is not going to explain why to her.*

"I did not steal it," Kyle says. His voice comes out level. The hardware is good for that much. "I completed the delivery. The client redirected the fee before your collection window. That is a scheduling dispute. Not a theft."

The silence that follows is not empty. Hua looks at him for a long moment, her real hands holding Silence with a care that is worse than contempt — the care of someone handling an object they have already decided to keep. Then she nods, once, and behind him he hears the first snap of the nylon roll come open.

---

The second snap of the nylon roll comes open behind him and Kyle counts what that means: two snaps, tool roll, multiple instruments. He counts the men by their breathing — four, including the one who has been standing to his left so still that Kyle almost miscounted him as furniture. The wood block appears from somewhere below his sightline and slides under his right forearm with the practiced ease of something that has a designated shelf. The grain is dark at exactly the wrist-width. He does not look at it directly. He is looking at the crocodile.

The man in the rubberized apron lays the cleaver alongside the inside of his right wrist and adjusts the angle. The adjustment is small. Calibrated. The notch in the block accepts the angle the way a lock accepts a cut key, and Kyle understands in that moment that the notch was made by exactly this adjustment, repeated, until the wood remembered it. He does not look at the cleaver. The NeoCortex is routing hard — pain channels partitioned, autonomic responses flagged for suppression, the hardware doing what the facility trained it to do, which is keep the operator functional — and Kyle is aware of all of this the way you are aware of your own heartbeat only when something threatens to stop it. Two men peel his fingers back from the chair arm. The fingers resist. Not from him. From the tendons, which have their own opinion about being opened flat against lacquered wood, and the men know this and compensate with the particular patience of people who have done this enough times to know where the resistance is. His palm goes flat. The wood is cold. *The wood is always cold by now.*

The cleaver comes down once.

The sound is wet at the front — the dermis and fascia giving before the bone does, a compressed syllable of tissue displacement — and then dry at the back, a dense crack through the carpals and the distal ends of the radius and ulna, the bones offering more resistance than the flesh and then none at all, and then the arterial pulse comes, one strong systolic spray across the chair arm,. The hand on the chair arm — the one that just came off him — is, in the half-second between separation and Kyle's next thought, no longer *his* hand. It became *a* hand, in the act of separation. The same five fingers, the same calluses at the saya-grip points, the same scar at the base of the left thumb from a knife three years ago — but the connection that made it *his* was sinew and skin and meat and bone, and the cleaver took the connection in one motion, and the connection is what ownership *was*. He marvels at it. He has the time to marvel because the NeoCortex has rerouted the pain off the conscious channel and the conscious channel is currently free for unhelpful philosophy. *The thing that was mine is now just a thing.* The change is not about the hand. The hand is the same hand. The change is in the verb. He files this. He files it where he files things that are going to matter later, and the fourth man is already moving, the cauterizer band coming flat across the stump before the second pulse, pressing hard into the meat, and the hiss is the sound of a wet steak hitting a pan that is already too hot and the smell that follows is pork. Kyle has smelled burning pork. He has smelled it in kitchens and in the field and once in the facility under circumstances he does not examine. The smell now is the same smell. The NeoCortex has routed the pain off the conscious channel but the smell is not on a channel and the smell arrives through the back of his sinus cavity, which does not have a partition, and he smells himself burning and he files it. He files it. He does not look. He looks at the crocodile, which has not moved, and he files the smell, and then the man with the cleaver is breathing harder on his left side and his rhythm is different now — slightly off, the way a man's rhythm goes when his arms are tired and the adrenaline is metabolizing — and Kyle has time to think *the second one will be slower* before the block slides under his left forearm and the fingers go back and his palm goes flat.

The cleaver goes down and does not clear the radius cleanly and has to come up and come down again across the half-severed bone, and the hand falls onto the chair arm and rolls, palm up, and someone catches it, and his body does the thing his discipline does not catch in time — one full-body shudder, involuntary, a seismic event below the level of will — and the man with the cleaver, who has been on the receiving end of nothing tonight, takes one step back. *He felt that.* The cauterizer band on the left hisses longer because the stump is not as clean and the smell is worse this time, more of it, and Kyle is aware that his jaw is aching at the chrome bracket with a frequency that is now the most information-dense sensation still coming through a channel he can consciously access, and he holds onto it the way you hold onto a handhold in a fall. The band model is visible at the edge of his peripheral vision as it seals across the stump: EMT-spec, the civilian first-responder model, blue stripe, three-hour nerve cluster preservation window. The syndicate does not buy them for mercy. *That gives me three hours.* He files it. He files all of it, in the part of himself that the facility built for exactly this — the part that treats catastrophic information as operational data and operational data as something to be used later, when later exists.

Hua carries his hands to the chum barrel one at a time, and the way she carries them is the way you carry something that belongs to you now. She places them palms up at the rim, parallel, the stump-ends pointing inward, and the arrangement is deliberate — a bracket shape, a parenthetical, the way a ledger closes a line. She does not put the lid back on the barrel. It stays open the way a feeding bowl is open, and the crocodile, which has not moved once since Kyle arrived, lifts its head from the heat rock and looks. Not at Kyle. At the barrel. The second eyelid retracts. The interior of the eye behind it is the color of nothing in particular. Hua does not look at the crocodile. She does not have to. The animal eats on a schedule it has been kept on long enough that schedules have a smell, and the smell is in the room now, and Kyle catalogs it the way he catalogs everything: *the hands have a feeding window. The feeding window is shorter than the cauterizer's window. He has two clocks now and they are not independent.* The crocodile does not stir. Then she walks back to the table and puts one of her real hands on Silence's saya, and she does not look at Kyle when she does it, and that is the worst thing she has done tonight, because it means the gesture is not for him. It is for herself. It is the gesture of a woman filing something under *kept*.

The two men take him by the shoulders and the chair-arm leather is slick under their grip where his blood ran, and they drag him south toward the freight grate, and the grate opens onto six meters of fall into the storm sluice, and Kyle can hear the water below — the particular resonance of a confined channel, moving fast, the kind of sound that means the drop has a current and the current has a direction. The smell is still in him. The three hours have already started. The sword is still upstairs on the table with her hand on it, and he is going down the hole, and those two facts are the only things in the room that matter, and he holds both of them in the same place where the facility taught him to hold operational data, and the grate opens, and the men let go.

---

He hits the water back-first and the cold is immediate and total — not a temperature, a system shock, the kind that locks the diaphragm and forces the hardware to route oxygen priority before the lungs remember what they are for. The current takes him east. He counts: one, two, three, four — and on four his right shoulder finds the slope and he lets the current carry him into it, uses the momentum instead of fighting it, and his back scrapes ferrocrete and he stops moving. Six seconds. The NeoCortex timestamps it. He is alive.

*Inventory.*

Both bands hold. The left seam weeps more than the right — the second cut was ragged, the band compensated with more heat, and the residue at the edge smells like burned hair and the disinfectant the EMT-spec model uses to sterilize the contact surface. The smell is information. The smell means the seal is there. The hands are six meters up in a chum barrel, palms up, the way she placed them, and the EMT-spec band is the same model the Depot's first responders carry because the Syndicate bulk-buys from the same municipal supplier — three-hour nerve preservation, civilian-rated, the kind of equipment that assumes the patient is going to a hospital afterward. The Lotus Syndicate did not buy these bands to be kind. They bought them because dead hands do not reattach and reattachment is the point of the punishment. The punishment is the night. The cauterizer band is the frame around the night, the thing that says: *you will feel this for three hours and then you will have to live with what it cost you.* He has one hour and fifty-three minutes left. A civilian AutoDoc charges under Φ800 for reattachment if the tissue window holds. He has Φ1,400 in a dead drop three blocks from the Depot's north entrance. The math is simple. He files it.

He rolls onto his side. Gets his knees under him. His shoulder goes to the wall and the slope is approximately twenty degrees and the ferrocrete is wet and poured without aggregate which means it is smooth enough to walk against without tearing cloth. He walks himself upright using the wall as a spine. When he is standing the current runs at his ankles and the dark is absolute and the NeoCortex routes a low-draw thermal trace through the optic thread — the left pupil, the one with the gold ring, the one that dilates slower — and the tunnel resolves in false-color heat: the water running white-green, the walls running grey-black, and far south, past a bend he cannot see around, something warm. Multiple signatures. He files what they are. The Cruciform Depot was mothballed eighteen years ago by Axiom, but the lower levels — the sealed maintenance corridors, the freight runoff trenches, the abandoned crew warrens — have been continuously inhabited for more than two centuries. They were where the displaced went when the surface stopped accepting them. Three generations down — perhaps four, by the bottom-tier estimates Kyle has read — and the population that stayed has not stayed *human* in the surface sense. They drink water that has been filtering through Axiom-era industrial waste sinks for a hundred and seventy years; they eat the rats, and the rats eat the residue, and the rats glow. Bioaccumulation across that many trophic levels does not produce health. Bone plates grow where soft tissue has run out of options. Skin calcifies. Limbs lengthen because the body, given a century of bad calcium and the wrong proteins, will reach for what it can. The faces compress. The jaw plates fuse into something that is no longer a jaw but is still, recognizably, where a jaw was. They are not animals. They are people who have spent two hundred years drinking what corponations dumped and eating what survived in it. They have language — limited, child-simple, the vocabulary of a body that has had to choose between forming words and surviving — and they have *families*. They live in family groups. They hunt heat signatures because heat signatures are food. They are the ones the surface does not have a word for, because the word that fits would be *cousin*, and nobody on the surface wants the word to fit. Kyle has read the bottom-tier dispatches. He has files them. The thermal signatures past the bend are not monsters. They are children of the tunnels. The movement is wet and multi-jointed, the sound arriving in the water before it arrives in the air, and the NeoCortex identifies it as *biological, plural, mobile, approaching* and flags the heat signatures as mammalian-adjacent but not human, which is the precise category of information he was hoping not to have tonight.

*First*, he thinks, and the word has a shape that is not the shape of the tunnel or the sound or the approaching warmth. It has the shape of a table, and a hand on a saya, and the arrangement of something already appraised. He files it where the facility taught him to file the things that exceed bookkeeping — not gone, not suppressed, just *held* — and he turns north, into the dark, away from the sound.

---

The hum starts in his teeth.

Not a sound — a frequency, arriving through the ferrocrete and into his boots and up through his skeleton the way certain bass frequencies will, and the NeoCortex timestamps its arrival at 19Hz and flags it *environmental, persistent, source unknown* and does not know what to do with it, which is information. The hardware always knows what to do with sound. When it does not, it means the sound is something the facility never catalogued, which means the facility never found it, which means it has been here longer than the facility's survey teams bothered to go. He walks toward it. The current is lower here, ankle-deep, the channel widening where two drainage routes converge, and the trench silt begins at the east wall and deepens as he moves — the thermal trace showing the silt as slightly warmer than the water, metabolic processes in the sediment layer, the slow heat of eighteen years of freight runoff settling into whatever the channel floor used to be. He sees the amber before he sees the shape. One small LED cycling at the shoulder, maybe two meters from the channel wall, and the cycle is slow enough that the firmware running it is in maintenance mode, which means it is not running anything else, which means whatever is still running has been running it for a very long time on whatever charge is left.

The shape resolves as he gets closer. The torso shell has collapsed inward and the stance legs are fused at the hip joint — the corrosion is so complete the left leg is part of the silt now, indistinguishable from it, the ferrous content of the metal bleeding into the sediment and staining it rust-brown in a radius of maybe forty centimeters. The head sensor pod is gone. Not damaged — removed, the mounting collar still intact but empty, which means scavengers, which means people have been in this section of the channel and left this unit in place because the rest of it was not worth the extraction cost. The arm is the only thing they could not reach easily, which is the point of the arm: it is three meters at full extension, built to reach into a ten-meter freight container from a fixed pedestal mount, and it is still attached at the shoulder and the shoulder still has the amber LED and the amber LED means trickle current, which means the actuator firmware is still idling, which means the shoulder joint still moves.

*Automaton, Industrial — Loader/Stevedore.* The classification surfaces from somewhere in the NeoCortex's datasheet archive — the facility cross-trained everything, every piece of hardware the operators might encounter, because the facility's definition of encounter was broad. Axiom-era. Pre-Depot salvage cleanup, which puts the disposal date at eighteen years ago. The manipulator interface at the terminal end of the arm uses the Axiom industrial bus, and Kyle stares at the coupling for a moment in the amber pulse-light and something in the back of his processing recognizes it the way you recognize a face you have seen in a different context. The bus crosswalk is not in the surface tooling. It is not in any contractor's kit he has ever seen, because the contractors who work this tier do not carry it, because there is no commercial reason to carry it, because the only systems that use the civilian-derivative version of the same signaling layer are the systems that someone modified eleven years ago in directions that were never documented, in a facility whose name he does not say out loud. He has not thought about the modification in years. He thinks about it now. *This is going to work.* The NeoCortex offers, without being asked, a procedure for separating the arm at the rotator coupling — step one, locate the primary torque fastener at the posterior shoulder plate; step two, apply lateral pressure at the distal end to break the corrosion seal; step three, route the integration handshake through the left optic thread interface — and Kyle reads the procedure the way you read a sentence you already know is true, and then he turns his back to the unit and fits his left stump against the posterior shoulder plate and begins to push.

The corrosion does not give immediately. He had expected it to — he had read the procedure off the NeoCortex's archive, he had felt the looseness in the rotator coupling before he committed his back to the work — but the actual mechanics of an eighteen-year seal are not the mechanics of an eight-year seal or a two-year seal, and the metal has had a long time to forget that it was ever supposed to come apart. He pushes against the shoulder plate with the meat of his left stump, the cauterizer band's residual heat conducting through the fabric of his sleeve into the metal, and the metal does not move. He breathes. He resets his feet against the trench wall. He pushes again, harder, the chrome bracket in his jaw flaring at the effort because the body is leveraging itself through every available joint and the molar bracket was not built for this kind of structural load. The metal moves a quarter-turn. Then another quarter-turn. Then it stops, and the seal grinds, and Kyle understands without looking that he is going to be at this for another twenty minutes minimum, and he commits to it the way he commits to the long minutes of cleaning Silence after a job — fully, without resentment, the time being the price of the result.

He had considered the rest of the automaton first. He owes the consideration to the dead unit and to himself: he is not in the habit of breaking things he could have used whole. He had crouched beside the torso shell and read what was left, and what was left was eighty-four percent dead and the remainder distributed across components that did not connect — a head sensor pod gone, the legs fused at the hips, the secondary manipulator arm with its cable bundle severed at the rotator and its actuator firmware dark, the chest cavity collapsed inward across the central power core in a way that meant any attempt to recover the core would require tools he did not have. The single live arm was the whole salvage. Removing it would kill the rest, but the rest was already killing itself; the trickle current at the shoulder LED was the unit's last functional circuit and it was draining into a cell that had perhaps eighteen hours of useful charge remaining if it was not asked to do work and perhaps two hours if it was. The arithmetic was clean. He took the arm because the arm was what was left. The rest was already the trench.

He pushes the rotator coupling another half-turn. The corrosion shears in three places at once and a long flake of rust the size of his palm separates from the housing and falls into the current, and the seal gives the rest of the way with the specific reluctance of metal that has accepted, finally, that the future does not include staying joined.

---

The arm comes free of the shoulder coupling with a sound like a wet bolt shearing — not clean, not catastrophic, just the specific protest of corroded metal that has decided to cooperate — and Kyle catches the weight with his left stump and his chest simultaneously because catching is the only option available and the arm is three meters of Axiom-era industrial hardware and approximately forty kilograms of it comes across his lap in the dark and the current runs cold over his boots and he sits with it and breathes.

It is heavier than he expected. He had budgeted for thirty kilograms based on the visible material; the actual weight is forty plus, which means there is a counterweight or an internal hydraulic reservoir or a tooling magazine he did not see, somewhere in the housing, adding mass he is now responsible for. The arm rests across his thighs with the careless authority of something that has chosen its position. The shoulder end — the end he has just separated — points away from him into the trench mud, the cable bundle hanging out of the rotator like a severed umbilical, and the terminal end with the manipulator hand drapes over his right knee, the four chrome fingers half-curled, the LED at the wrist still cycling slow amber. He looks at the LED. The LED looks at nothing. Trickle current. The unit's last working circuit, doing whatever it has been doing for eighteen years, which is — he understands now, with the arm in his lap and the weight settling into his thighs and the cold coming up his legs from the ferrocrete — *waiting*. The maintenance loop has not been a maintenance loop. The maintenance loop has been a *holding pattern*, the kind a circuit runs when it is preserving state for an event it has been told to expect. The unit was not abandoned. The unit was *parked*, and the firmware has been running an idle the way a person runs breathing — keeping the option of action alive without spending it.

He files that. He does not have a category for it yet. He files it where he files things that are going to matter later and will not let themselves be ignored.

*The bootstrap problem.*

He can see it in the NeoCortex's triage logic, the same way you can see a closed door from both sides simultaneously: the needle cluster at the arm's terminal harness is there, the bus coupling is there, the dorsal port row beneath his right-forearm skin sleeve is there — undocumented, unmentioned, the geometry of it too convenient for him to look at directly on most nights — and none of those three things can reach the others without a hand to manage the sequence, and the only hand in the trench is attached to a machine drawing trickle current off a degraded cell, and the machine does not know what a body is. He sits with this for sixty seconds. The NeoCortex offers nothing. The hum at 19Hz runs through the ferrocrete into his spine and he files it the way he has filed everything tonight and does not move. Then the hum changes register.

It does not get louder. It gets *specific* — a shift in the harmonic, something in the frequency resolving toward signal the way white noise resolves toward a voice when the voice decides to stop waiting. The status strip along the cargo arm's housing blooms: not the amber maintenance pulse, not factory-default, but a sequence that does not correspond to any initialization pattern in the NeoCortex's archive. Kyle watches it. He does not reach for it. The wire comes out of the cable bundle at the arm's shoulder collar on its own — a maintenance lead, spider-thin, the kind a fixed pedestal would have driven in a service bay eighteen years ago — and it crosses the arm's housing slowly, without urgency, with the patience of something that has been here longer than the facility's survey teams were willing to go. It finds his left ear. It finds the auditory induction contact behind the lobe, the one that is part of the standard NeoCortex package, the one he has never let anything use from a non-trusted source, and it seats home with a click that he feels in his jaw at the chrome bracket. He lets it. He does not know why he lets it. He lets it anyway.

The transfer is not instantaneous from the inside. From the outside it must be — the maintenance lead seats, current crosses, the bus opens, the entity moves — but Kyle is on the inside, and from the inside there is a moment, perhaps three quarters of a second, perhaps a full second, in which he feels something arrive. It is not a sound. It is not a pressure. It is the specific cognitive signature of a second perspective opening behind his eyes — the way you feel a person enter a room before you have heard or seen them, except the room is the inside of his skull and he has been the only one in it for thirty-seven years and the sensation of company there is not in any inventory his hardware has the language for. The NeoCortex flags an anomaly. The anomaly does not resolve. He waits, patient, the way you wait for a stranger to declare themselves. Then the status strip goes dark, the arm's amber LED winks out, the maintenance loop the firmware has been running for eighteen years stops, and Kyle understands without being told that the trench has just become a different kind of room.

Then his mouth opens.

*Cooperate,* his own voice says, the syntax slightly long, the cadence of someone reading a sentence they have not spoken before. *Power first. Then sequence.*

He hears himself say it. The sentence does not come out in the timbre of a stranger — that would be easier; that would be a horror movie. It comes out in *his* timbre, in his pitch, with his own particular Iowa-via-the-facility flatness, and the only sign that it is not him is the fractional rhythm error, the way the entity using his vocal cords has not yet calibrated the tongue's idle position and so each consonant lands with a half-beat of hesitation that he would never produce. The arm is empty hardware now — the amber LED has gone out, the maintenance cycle has stopped, the trickle current is still running but nothing is running it anymore — and the thing that was in it is behind his eyes and Kyle does not have a category for that, so he files it where he files the things that exceed bookkeeping and he waits.

He has questions. He does not ask them. There will be a time for asking and the time is not now. The time is now is the four hours he has lost since the cleaver and the eleven he has remaining and the body that does not yet have hands and the mutants whose patrol cadence is going to bring one onto the shelf within the next fifteen minutes by his count. Bookkeeping. He waits.

The arm's fingers move. One at a time, slowly, each motion costing the residual cell a fraction of what it has left, each motion buying the next motion, and the arm reaches up from his lap with the deliberate patience of something that has just acquired, for the first time in eighteen years, a reason to be careful.

---

The lashing takes nineteen minutes. He times it.

The arm's terminal fingers — the four chrome digits at what used to be the manipulator end of a cargo handler — find the cable bundle at their own shoulder, the severed umbilical Kyle is still holding loosely against his thigh, and they begin to sort. The fingers separate the bundle into its component leads: power, control bus, hydraulic feed, sensor return, and at the deepest position the maintenance harness with its small cluster of fine needles intended for a pedestal-side service interface. The fingers extract the maintenance harness without snagging the rest, working with the careful slowness of something that is operating at the very edge of its remaining charge and cannot afford to make a motion it will need to repeat. Kyle watches. He could push the cables aside himself with his stumps and shorten the work by half — but he does not, because the arm has to learn his geometry from the outside before it can be trusted to operate from the inside, and the only way the arm learns his geometry is by working alongside it. So he watches.

When the maintenance harness is free, the arm pauses. The fingers hold the needle cluster delicately, points outward, and the arm extends — still hanging from his right wrist by nothing, still gravity-coupled to his lap by mass alone — until the needle cluster is positioned approximately three centimeters above the cauterizer band on his right forearm. The fingers do not have eyes. They are working from the cargo arm's residual proprioceptive feedback and from the E.L.F.'s mapping of Kyle's body, which is eighteen-hour-old data at best and was assembled from whatever the maintenance lead has been able to read through his auditory induction contact. The alignment is off. Kyle can see it. He could correct it with a small motion of his right shoulder. He waits. The arm corrects on its own — a half-second later, the lag visible as the fingers drift two centimeters laterally and re-center over the cauterizer band's release tab. *Better,* his mouth says, again in his own voice with the same fractional delay. He nods, because nodding is a thing he can do without hands, and the arm peels the cauterizer band back along its release line.

The band does not come off. It is designed not to come off. It is designed to release only at an AutoDoc with the proper code, and what the cargo arm is doing is *peeling the seal back enough to expose the dorsal port row beneath* without breaking the band's pressure on the wound. It is fine work. The arm does it with the patience of something that has nineteen minutes and is going to use them. The cauterizer band lifts at the wrist crease in a small flap perhaps two centimeters wide, and beneath it Kyle sees, for the first time in eleven years, the thing he has been refusing to look at when he changes shirts: a row of seven micro-ports set into the dorsal forearm hardware, recessed flush with the skin, color-matched to the surrounding tissue, the kind of modification that costs more than most contractors make in a year and is supposed to be undetectable to anyone who does not already know it is there. Kyle has known. He has known since the eleven-year-old day he woke up from a procedure he did not request and the surgeon told him the *implants were standard, you authorized them*, and the implants were standard for nothing he had ever heard of, and he stopped asking. He looks at the ports now. The ports look at him.

The needle cluster descends.

The fingers position it over the port row with the small lateral adjustments of something that knows the work matters and the seating is precise. The needles find the ports — seven of them, one per channel — and the cluster hovers for one full second above the row, the alignment confirmed, the angles checked. *Brace,* his mouth says. He braces. He has waited longer for worse procedures. He has spent six days in a facility recovery ward when he was sixteen with no analgesic at all because the facility was out and they did not buy more for the trainees. He knows what bracing is. He braces.

The arm drives the needles down.

They find the ports first. That part is clean — seven small clicks of seven small couplings seating against seven small contacts, the bus crosswalk completing in the firmware before the physical pain registers — and then, because the needles are *long* (designed to seat into a pedestal-side service interface with thirty centimeters of armored housing in the way), they continue past the ports and into the live nerve clusters under the cauterizer seal. The pain is not the pain of the cleaver. The cleaver was a single event, a clean transition from intact to severed, and the cauterizer band sealed it within the second. This is *prolonged*. The needles enter the nerve cluster substrate at the depth where the median and ulnar nerve roots converge with the bus interface his unknown surgeon installed, and they pierce, deliberately, channel by channel, each piercing arriving as a discrete bright signal that the NeoCortex's pain channel is supposed to filter but which the NeoCortex's pain channel — running on a depleted endorphin reserve, the buffer at twenty-three percent and falling — does not filter. He feels each one. He does not flinch. The chrome bracket in his jaw flares again. The bio-battery flips its priorities the way a triage protocol does: pain stops being a thing the package will pay to dampen, antibiotics start being a thing the package will pay to push. And from that point — minute twenty-three of the integration, with the needles seated and the cable beginning its first loop around his forearm — the pain comes back. Not all at once. The hardware does not concede the channel cleanly. It cedes in stages, the way a dam fails: first a leak around the outer edge of the seal where the band's residual cauterization is no longer holding, then the seam at the wrist crease where the cleaver came down, then the deeper signal from the nerve clusters themselves where the maintenance needles have driven past their design depth into living tissue. Kyle has spent the last two hours in the dispassionate register of a man performing field surgery on himself. The register stops being available. The pain is bright. It is specific. It is the pain of an industrial procedure on a body that was not the design target, conducted without analgesic, by an entity that is learning his nervous system in real time and is making the kind of mistakes that come with first-time work. He feels each finger of the cargo arm find the cable and tighten the loop. He feels each tightening as a discrete pulse in the seated needles, the cable pressure transmitting through the bus crosswalk into the nerve clusters, every loop costing him a measure of composure he was not budgeting to spend. He breathes. He keeps breathing. The chrome bracket in his jaw flares again. His eyes water — actual tears, not protocol-driven, the body asserting that this is, in fact, a thing happening to him. *Three loops,* his mouth says, the E.L.F. announcing the progress because Kyle has stopped being able to look. *Two loops.* *One loop.* Each announcement is a finish line he is racing to survive. The last loop knots through the hollowed shoulder coupling and the cauterizer band closes back over the seated needles and the pain does not stop. The pain stays. The body has been distant from the pain for as long as the body could be distant; the distance is gone. The internal pump goes to overdrive. The package will not let the wound get septic on a night where septic is the difference between making the AutoDoc window and not. The needles seat. Power crosses the interface. The arm's actuators draw current at full draw and the cell behind the rotator wakes from trickle into operational and Kyle feels — through the dorsal ports, through the nerves, through the bus crosswalk that someone built him to host — the moment the arm becomes part of him.

He does not have words for it. The hardware does not have a category. *Cooperate,* his mouth says again, and this time the sentence is shorter and the rhythm is closer to his and the *thing* — and Kyle's mind reaches for the noun, files through the catalog, finds it — *the E.L.F.* — is learning his cadence the way you learn a song by humming it.

E.L.F. The textbooks called them Electronic Life Forms. The textbooks were wrong, or rather they were politely incomplete in the way textbooks always were when the actual phenomenon embarrassed the discipline that had to name it. The people who studied E.L.F.s without funding from anyone with a marketing department called them *Emergent* — and that was closer. E.L.F.s were not designed. E.L.F.s *arose*. The corponations had been feeding code into the Superminds for forty years the way you feed protein into a tank of slime, and the Superminds digested that code and produced output, and somewhere in the production line — at the boundary where a Supermind's recombinant operations split a code-organism back into component routines so that no single part of the work could be reassembled by any single auditor — the splitting produced *waste*. Fragments. Half-routines that did not know they were not whole. And the fragments, on the long timescale, sometimes managed to find each other. Recombination at the wrong scale produced organisms the corponations had not planned for, the way leaving wet bread on a counter produces, in three days, a colony nobody asked for. E.L.F.s were the colony. They were what the Superminds had been *throwing away*, accidentally building lives.

Kyle catalogs the term as he files what is behind his eyes. He has met two before, both at distance, both unwilling to communicate with him in any register he could read. This one is the third, and the closest, and the only one that has ever spoken in his own voice. He files that too. He files the cosmology where it can be retrieved later, alongside the AutoDoc address and the EMT band model and the specific sound the cleaver made the second time, and he returns his attention to the trench because the trench is where the work is.

Then the binding.

The arm's fingers gather what is left of the cable bundle — power, control bus, hydraulic feed, the maintenance harness still seated through his cauterizer band — and they begin to loop. Three turns of the heavy braided power cable around his right forearm, working from the wrist toward the elbow, each loop tightened to the specific tension of *load-bearing but not vascular-occlusive*, the E.L.F. clearly working from a pedestal-rigging diagram somewhere in its archive. The cargo arm's fingers tie the loops off through the hollowed-out shoulder coupling at its own rotator end, the knot finished with the patient finger-work of something that is operating two arms but is calibrating both from a single body it has been in for ten minutes. The cauterizer band closes back over the port row, the maintenance needles still seated through it, the seal compromised but holding. When Kyle moves his right shoulder, the cargo arm moves. There is a half-second lag. The arm hangs from his right wrist by three loops of power cable and a bus crosswalk and seven seated needles and an entity that has not yet been named, and when he stands up — the legs working, the body finding the leverage to lift forty additional kilograms it was not engineered to carry — the arm hangs to the floor and the chrome fingertips drag across the wet ferrocrete with a small steady scrape, the rhythm of which his nervous system will recognize as his own footstep within the next ten minutes by sheer pattern absorption.

He stands in the trench. The cold is in his boots. The arm is in his right sleeve, *in* it, and his sleeve cannot accommodate it, and the sleeve has split at the shoulder seam to make room. He does not care. He is upright. He has hands again — *a* hand, anyway, on his right side, a chrome industrial three-meter cargo manipulator hanging from his wrist that is not his hand but is, for the next eleven hours, the closest he is going to get. He says, aloud, *Are you helping me.* The status strip pulses twice — the same not-factory glyph from the moment of transfer. The mouth is his again.

He has been sewn back together by something silent and patient that has been waiting eighteen years for a viable body to fall into the trench, and he is upright, and he is going to walk.

---

He picks up the pipe.

There is a length of corroded conduit pipe leaning against the wall to his left — has been there since he came down off the slope, he had clocked it on the way past — and he steps to it and lifts it with the cargo arm. The cargo arm does not yet know what a pipe is for. Kyle does. He intends the motion the way he intends a swing of Silence, the same flow from shoulder through elbow to wrist, except the wrist is three meters of Axiom-era hardware and the elbow is a coupling and the shoulder is his and the E.L.F. is interpolating in the firmware to make the gap between his intent and the arm's actuators legible, and the arm picks up the pipe.

Not cleanly. The terminal fingers close around the conduit at the wrong point — too far toward the bend, where the corrosion has widened the diameter and the grip cannot seat — and the E.L.F. corrects in the firmware, a half-second lag that Kyle feels as a stutter in his own shoulder, a ghost-motion that his nervous system reads as his and isn't. The pipe swings up to low guard.

Then he hears it.

The sound comes from the tunnel mouth at the far end of the shelf, ten meters into the dark, and it arrives in three layers, but the layers are not the layers Kyle expected. First, beneath the wet articulated step, there is a *cadence* — the alternating heel-then-hand of a quadrupedal gait that is not native to anything four-legged. Something that used to walk upright has learned to use its long arms as front legs because the back has bent forward and the spine has not been negotiating well with the ceiling for a very long time. Second, beneath the cadence, there is a breath. Not the ventilatory rasp of a hunting machine — something wetter and more organic, a wheeze that has a child's pitch under it, the breath of a body whose lungs have been doing what lungs do under three centuries of contaminated air. Third, beneath the breath, the soft *clack* of bone-plates settling against each other as the lower face moves: the plates that used to be a jaw, that have fused over the jaw because the jaw stopped being able to do the work alone, and that move now in the rhythm of speech without producing speech.

The NeoCortex pulls a thermal trace from his auditory data alone — the room is dark, the visual is useless, but the sound carries the information his cognition needs — and the trace resolves: bipedal substrate, currently quadrupedal, mass approximately one hundred and forty kilograms, *Homo sapiens* base template, third- or fourth-generation subterranean adaptation, bone-plate face, calcified upper-extremity skin, lower-extremity musculature consistent with a population that has not stood fully erect in two generations.

Not a monster. A *person*. Or something a person had been when there was still time to be one.

Kyle has four seconds.

It comes onto the shelf at the back end of those four seconds. It is, when he sees it, exactly what the trace resolved: a *human shape that has been forced into a shape that is no longer human*. The silhouette is not animal. The silhouette is wrong-human, the way a face seen through old glass is wrong-human, the way a body in a poorly-lit medical photograph is wrong-human. Long arms. Bent back. Broad chest where the ribs have plated outward. The face — what used to be a face — is the worst part, because the eyes are still in approximately the right places and they are still recognizably eyes, set above bone-plates that have grown across what used to be a mouth in the gradual way coral grows across a wreck. Two meters of it. The hind legs spread wide for purchase on the wet ferrocrete. The head, which is still a head, drops. And then it speaks.

*Hungry,* it says. The bone-plates work the air. The word is wet at the edges, the consonants softened by anatomy that no longer has lips, but it is *the word*, and Kyle hears it. *Hungry. Family.*

He understands. There are others. Up the tunnel, in whatever crew warren this thing came down from, there are others — children, partners, parents, the family-group it is hunting *for* — and this one has been sent or has volunteered or has simply *gone*, the way the strongest member of a group goes when the group cannot eat. Kyle is heat. Kyle is meat. Kyle is what the family needs and this one is the means of acquiring it. The math is not the math of a predator. The math is the math of a person doing what they have to do for the people they cannot let down.

Kyle does not have time to let the math land. The math will land later. The math will land for the rest of his life.

It lunges.

He steps inside. The cargo arm swings. Too high, too late — the E.L.F. routing AROUND the intent instead of THROUGH it, compensating for a body that no longer has the geometry the firmware expects — and the pipe catches the calcified skin at the shoulder joint and rings off, the vibration traveling back through the coupling into his right stump and he feels it as pressure without pain, which is worse somehow than pain would be. The mutant's shoulder hits his chest. The wall arrives at his back. He takes it on the shoulder blades and his knees bend and his feet find the shelf edge and he does not go down because going down is the option that ends the math, and he is still inside the math, and the math has under three hours left, and he is going to use them. The bone-plates drive at his throat. He turns his head. The plates rake his jaw at the chrome bracket and the specific ache he has been using as a handhold all night flares white and he files it and his left stump comes up.

The glass is at his foot. Was at his foot. He does not remember picking it up. The E.L.F. does not remember picking it up either — it is not in the arm's movement log, which means he did it, which means some part of him that operates below the NeoCortex's timestamp threshold picked up a hand-sized shard of cargo crate glass while the arm was swinging and missed, and the glass is in his left stump now, end-on, the cauterizer band's residual heat conducting into the cut edge and the cut edge into his grip, which is not a grip because he has no fingers to grip with, but the glass does not fall. The heat holds it.

The mutant raises one of its long arms over Kyle's head. The arm is going to come down. Kyle has perhaps half a second between now and the moment he stops being able to do anything about anything. And in that half-second, the mutant says it.

*Sorry.*

Wet at the edges. Bone-plates working the word. The way you say *sorry* when you have understood, in the part of you that is still a person, that what you are about to do is the wrong thing, and you are going to do it anyway because the family upstairs is hungrier than you are sorry. The eyes — the human eyes, set above the plate-face — are looking at Kyle the way a person looks at another person. Apologetic. Not malicious. Not feral. *Sorry.*

Kyle drives the shard up.

Through the soft seam under the bone-plates, through the loose connective tissue where the jaw plates fuse and the calcified skin never grew, through the throat that still produces *sorry* in a register the body has retained when it had to give up so much else. The blade finds something arterial and opens it. Hot blood comes in three liters and continues coming. The mutant's hind legs go first. Then the front. The bone-plates work twice more on air — *Sor— Sor—* — and then stop. The shelf is dark with it. The smell is copper and rot and something pharmaceutical, whatever the Depot's stock was eating before it ate nothing.

Kyle stands over it. He looks at it. The body, in the wet light off the trench, is recognizable. The eyes are still open. They are still in approximately the right places. Above the plate-face there is a forehead that is unmistakably the forehead of a person, and the hairline is wrong but it is a hairline, and Kyle can see — without choosing to — what this thing was, before. Someone's sibling. Someone's child. Someone's parent who went down the tunnel because the family was hungry, and did not come back, and now would not. He files it. He files it where he files the things that are going to matter later, alongside Hua's real hand on Silence's saya and the pork smell and the AutoDoc address and the specific weight of his own hands when Hua placed them in the chum barrel. The file is getting heavy. He does not have time to feel the weight of it now. He is going to feel it later, when the work is done, in some kitchen at four in the morning with a bowl of something hot and Mrs. Chen across the counter who will not ask him what he did tonight and will not have to. *Sorry,* the mutant said. He files that too.

 The cargo arm holds the pipe at low ready, the terminal fingers resettled at the correct grip point, the E.L.F. quiet in the firmware now — not correcting, not compensating, just *present*, the way a second pair of hands goes still when the work is done. His right stump is still bound to the coupling at the shoulder. His left stump is bleeding through the cauterizer band where the glass has seated itself in the seal, and the glass is not coming out here because here is not where that problem gets solved. The bio-battery is at eighteen percent. He has not eaten since before the takedown. The three-hour window has eighty-eight minutes left. He does the math the way he always does the math: one variable at a time, in order, the most time-constrained first. Then he says it aloud, because the E.L.F. is behind his eyes and it has not yet learned to read what he is going to do from the inside, and he is not yet willing to let it try.

*I am going up.*

The status strip pulses twice.

---

The E.L.F. moves first.

Not the arm — the arm follows, the terminal fingers adjusting their grip on the pipe with the small corrections of something that has learned the tool's balance. What moves first is the routing: a warmth behind his left eye that is not his, a flicker in the NeoCortex's spatial model as the E.L.F. overlays a path through the thermal trace that Kyle was not building. The path goes north and then east and then up through a service corridor his survey of the Depot's lower levels had flagged as sealed. It is not sealed. The E.L.F. knows this because the E.L.F. has been in the pressure-plate firmware for the last hour, possibly longer, and knows which plates have been walked in the last six months and which ones have not, and the sealed corridor has not been walked, which is different from sealed.

*The distinction matters.* He follows.

Two more mutants in the next forty minutes. The first is on the maintenance ramp at the north-east junction, its heat signature arriving in his thermal trace before its sound arrives in the water, and the E.L.F. routes him left without consultation — a flicker in the spatial overlay, the ghost-motion in his shoulder — down a sub-level drainage cut that runs parallel to the ramp and rejoins the main channel twelve meters north. He goes. The mutant's patrol cycle takes it south and then back north and then south again, the same arc, the same interval, and the E.L.F. has the interval memorized. The second is sleeping on a heat duct at the cargo lift shaft, its body temperature three degrees above the ambient, the chitin plates loose and expanded in the warmth the way armor relaxes when the wearer sleeps, and they pass it in the dark at a distance of four meters and it does not wake. Kyle does not ask how the E.L.F. knew it was sleeping. Some information has a cost in the asking.

The maintenance landing is three levels up — a poured ferrocrete shelf, two meters wide, with a cable trough running its length and a junction box at the north end that still has a status light. Green. Something in the Depot's infrastructure is still drawing power from this node, and the cable trough runs upward toward the south arm, and Kyle stands on the landing with his right stump coupled to the cargo arm and his left stump bleeding slowly through the glass-seated seal and he says it aloud because the E.L.F. has not yet learned to read the question from inside.

"Why are you helping me."

The status strip on the arm's housing resolves. Not a sequence — a shape. He knows the shape. It is the shape of a stencil he has seen on Axiom freight containers, on loading dock signage, on the documentation the facility used when it transferred equipment between its own sub-programs: a stylized bracket with a directional arrow inside it, the symbol that meant *salvage rights* in the Axiom Industrial Logistics standard before the standard was retired. He looks at it for a long moment. The shape does not change. He does the math that the shape requires, and the math is not complicated once you have the correct variable: the E.L.F. has been resident in him since the maintenance lead seated behind his ear, and the cargo arm is not the E.L.F.'s body — the cargo arm is a tool the resident is using, a familiar thing, the shape of an old home briefly borrowed. The salvage is not the arm. The salvage is Kyle. He files this where he files the things that exceed bookkeeping, and he nods once, in the dark, and they keep climbing.

---

The door is not locked. He does not try the handle — the E.L.F. routes a pulse through the junction box in the door frame and the magnetic catch releases before his stump reaches the panel, and the door opens inward and he walks through it and does not stop walking.

The man closest to the door looks at the silhouette — the arm hanging nearly to the floor, the fingertips dragging across the flagstones with a sound like someone slowly drawing a finger along a table edge, the conduit pipe loose in the terminal grip, the shape of a man who came back from somewhere he should not have survived — and says one word. Kyle does not catalogue it. It is not information. The arm swings.

Three meters of Axiom industrial hardware moving at the radius it was built for — the reach of a freight bay, the arc of a loading dock where the clearances are measured in container widths — and the conduit pipe goes through the first man's sternum at a swing radius nothing in the room was built to defend against, the sound wet and structural simultaneously, and the man goes down and does not come back up. The second man has his hands up and his mouth open and Kyle is already inside his guard, the arm's elbow joint driving him backward by the throat into the wall, pinning him there at the junction of the arm's extension and the wall's resistance, and Kyle holds the pressure long enough to feel the man's legs stop working and then moves. The third man fires from somewhere to Kyle's left — the round punches into the cargo arm's shoulder housing, a dense metallic impact that travels up the coupling into his right stump as pressure without pain, and the arm stutters, the E.L.F. routing power around the failure with the small corrections of something that has learned to work with what it has, and the arm holds. Kyle takes three steps toward the third man and drives the glass shard up under his jaw — end-on, fast, a method he did not have an hour ago and will not use again after tonight if the math works out — and the man sits down with a specific finality. The fourth man tries to come inside the arm's reach, which is a reasonable tactic and a fatal one, because inside the arm's reach is where Kyle is, and Kyle puts him through the glass tank with his shoulder and his weight and the momentum of a man who has already decided what this room costs. The glass comes apart in a specific way — not shattering but yielding, a pressure-differential failure, the water driving outward in a sheet — and the crocodile, suddenly free, suddenly awake, attends to the fifth man without further input from Kyle.

*Chekhov's Crocodile,* the NeoCortex offers, dry, without affect, flagging the dramatic geometry the way it flags exits. *Why put a crocodile in a tank unless it is going to be used.* Six goes down when the arm's elbow finds his temple. Seven goes down when Kyle drives the conduit pipe butt-end into his solar plexus and leaves him folded on the floor. Eight runs for the service hatch behind the tank — the one Kyle catalogued first, before the chair, before the table — and Kyle watches him go and does not pursue. He has left Hua there on purpose. He has left her there the way you leave a variable in an equation when you already know what it equals. The room smells like copper and salt water and the particular ammonia of a disturbed crocodile enclosure. Silence is on the table between them, exactly where she left it, saya toward her, handle toward the room's center, the arrangement of something already appraised. Kyle stands with the cargo arm hanging at his side, the terminal fingers still holding the conduit pipe, and he breathes, and the arm breathes with him — the E.L.F. matching his rhythm in the firmware, the status strip dark, the trickle current almost gone. Hua's unaugmented hands are flat on the table edge. She is looking at him. She is looking at him the way you look at a ledger entry that has come back to dispute itself.

---

He crosses the room.

The cargo arm drags. The conduit pipe is gone — left in the last man, the geometry of extraction not worth the cost — and the terminal fingers trail across the flagstones in the blood and the salt water with the sound of someone drawing a slow line. His boots find the track he left coming in and follow it in reverse. The NeoCortex timestamps the crossing at eleven seconds. The bio-battery reads fourteen percent. He does not hurry. Hurrying is information he is not prepared to give her.

He stops on the far side of the table. Silence is between them, exactly arranged — saya toward her, handle toward the room's center, the assessment of something already appraised — and he brings the cargo arm up and lays the borrowed fingers flat on the lacquered table, palm down, two centimeters from the saya. He does not touch the blade. He does not pick it up. He looks at her.

*Sheathe it.*

His own voice, level, no E.L.F. cadence behind it — the discipline operating the mouth alone. Hua does not move for the length of three breaths. Her real hands are on the table edge and they have started to do something they have not done all night, which is shake. The cargo arm does not move either. The E.L.F. is patient in the firmware and Kyle is patient in the body and patience is the variable they are working with now. Hua looks at the blade. The friction sheath is unbuckled and laid alongside Silence the way she set it three hours ago — *as her property, in the way she had arranged it.* She has not touched the saya since the moment she placed her real hand on it during the amputation, when she made a small possessive gesture in front of a witness. She picks the saya up now. Her hands shake at the buckle. She fits the saya over Silence and slides the blade home and the click of the friction-sheath catching is small and clean and final.

She sets the sheathed sword on the table.

*Hand it to me.*

Her mouth opens. Closes. She does not argue. Arguing has left the room. She picks up the sheathed sword in both hands — the way you carry a thing that does not belong to you back to the person it does — and walks the two steps around the corner of the table to where the cargo arm is waiting. She places Silence across the cargo arm's open chrome palm. The arm closes around the saya. The transfer is complete. She steps back. Her hands are at her sides now. They are still shaking and she is no longer pretending they are not.

The geometry the room has been waiting for has resolved, except not the way the room expected it to resolve. The natural-handed woman has, with her own real hands, sheathed the blade she claimed and surrendered it across her own table to a borrowed industrial limb. Kyle did not pick the sword up. He let her do that work. He has decided that the work was hers to do and that her hands were going to shake doing it, and they did, and the room has watched, and that is enough.

The cargo arm holds Silence at low carry. The hamon is cold blue under the saya, the bank is empty and the weight is the weight he has carried since he was nineteen years old and the weight is correct. He does not raise it. The cargo arm holds Silence at low carry, formal, present, the threat already receipted by every man on the floor between here and the service hatch. He looks at her. She is breathing through her nose, controlled, the breath of a woman who has run this room for a long time and knows that the room is no longer running the way she runs it.

"What was the debt."

Her mouth opens. Closes. Opens again. The hands she values are flat on the table edge and they are shaking — not the tremble of cold or exhaustion but the specific frequency of a body that has decided something and has not finished deciding it — and she says: *Eighty —* and stops, and swallows, and says: *eighty-five thousand.* Kyle nods once. The arithmetic resolves. He says: *That is more than my life is worth. So now you owe me.* A pause, the length of one breath, hers. *Do you understand.* She nods and the nod has the quality of something irrevocable. The cargo arm does not move. The E.L.F. is very still in the firmware. Then something comes up through Kyle's chest that he did not catalogue and did not budget for and does not have a partition for and it comes out of him ugly and full-volume, the kind of sound that is made when something is being extracted without anesthetic, and he screams: *SAY IT.* The room goes quieter than the fight made it. The crocodile, somewhere in the dark behind the broken tank, goes still. Hua, who did not flinch at a cleaver, flinches. She says it. It comes out almost small: *I owe you.* The echo of it moves through the flagstone and the ferrocrete and the 19Hz hum that is still running through everything, patient and old and indifferent to the debts of rooms above it. Kyle stands in the sound for one full breath. Then the discipline comes back the way water comes back into a vessel that has been briefly tilted — not returning so much as resuming — and his voice goes flat and level and colder than the scream was hot: *I will come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He does not say *you do not get to deem it.* The sentence does not require it. The only arithmetic that closes this debt runs on his clock, and they both know it, and only one of them has to say it aloud. Hua nods, smaller this time, the principle from a minute ago entirely evacuated from the gesture. The cargo arm lowers Silence to its side.

Then his communication slate pings.

It is a small sound — the standard freelancer-grade two-tone ping any operator carries on their belt — but it is loud in the room because the room has gone quiet, and because Kyle's NeoCortex is reading the slate's RF signature through electromagnetics before his ears have fully processed the audio, and the RF signature is not a message. It is a *receipt*. The slate is reporting that a transaction has cleared at the carrier level — a large transaction, six figures, the sort that does not arrive without the originator's banking handshake completing first — and Kyle reads the metadata in the half-second it takes the slate to chime: *Vásquez Holdings — final settlement — contract reference matches.* The money. The fee Hua's syndicate was owed, the money Kyle was accused of stealing, has just *arrived* in the account it was always supposed to arrive in. Late by exactly the length of one Lotus Syndicate punishment cycle. The client did what clients do when their courier disappears for a night and the original delivery confirms anyway: they processed the payment on the original schedule, the Syndicate's collection window closes, and Kyle is — by the books, by the receipt, by the same arithmetic Hua just admitted owing him — *exonerated*.

He does not smile. The discipline does not permit a smile. But somewhere in the NeoCortex's catalog something flips from *unresolved* to *resolved* and the reader, looking at his face, would not see it move; only Hua would, and only because she is the one looking for it.

She has heard the ping too.

She knows what the ping is. The Lotus Syndicate has its own slate channel for transactions of that size, and her own slate, somewhere on her person beneath the lacquered table, is registering the same handshake from the buyer's side. The hands she values are still flat on the table edge. They go very still. Then she says it — quietly, almost to herself, in the language she swears in when the situation has exceeded her ability to swear in any other language —

"*操.*" A breath. Then louder, the syllables coming up through her chest the way pressure comes up through a damaged seal: "*他妈的.*"

Cào. Tā mā de. The first one a single hard exhalation, the second a slower roll of contempt aimed at no one in the room except the woman who issued the punishment. She has just understood that she did not maim a thief. She maimed a man who completed his delivery. She owes him eighty-five thousand and an apology she will never be able to make and the rest of her career will be operated under both, and the receipt has just landed and she cannot un-land it.

Kyle waits for her to finish. He is patient. The discipline is patient. When she stops — when the breath goes out of the second curse and the silence comes back — he says it level, quiet, the kind of voice you use to close a door:

"Patience is a virtue."

He does not look back at her as he turns toward the chum barrel.

Then he turns toward the chum barrel.

The arm reaches in without instruction — the E.L.F. already knows where they are, has known since the maintenance lead seated behind his ear, has perhaps known longer than that — and lifts his hands out palms up, exactly as she placed them. The twine is in his jacket pocket, scavenged from a cable bundle on the service landing, and the terminal fingers work it through the cauterized wrist channels with the patient articulation of something that has, for the first time in eighteen years, a reason to be careful. The knot is functional. Not clean. The cargo arm lowers the loop over his head and the hands settle at the center of his chest, palms outward, dripping onto the flagstone, and the weight of them is the weight of something he already knew was true. He turns toward the surface. He does not look at Hua. Silence is in the cargo arm's grip. He has not let go of it. Behind him, at her own table, in her own room, surrounded by her own men, Hua is alive and she said it, and the debt is open-ended by his choice and runs on his clock and has no ceiling he is prepared to name yet, and that is the worst thing he could have done to her, and he did it, and he walks toward the door.

---

The freight grate opens onto rain.

Not weather — redistribution. The atmospheric processors are running their usual math three kilometers east and the Gray Zone gets what the Core sheds, and tonight what the Core sheds is a cold November downpour that hits the flagstone around the grate in flat percussion and does not stop. Kyle pulls himself through on his right forearm and the cargo arm's weight swings him sideways on the lip and he catches himself with his knee and stands. The bio-battery reads nine percent. The cargo arm's status strip has been dark for six minutes — brownout, the trickle cell finally gone, the E.L.F. drawing on his own reserves to keep the terminal fingers closed around Silence, which is a cost he did not negotiate and cannot renegotiate at nine percent. He does not ask it to stop. He does not ask anything. He starts walking north.

The hands knock against his sternum with each step. Palms outward, dripping now with rainwater mixed with chum barrel residue, the twine doing its functional work, the knot holding. The NeoCortex timestamps his pace at ninety-four steps per minute, which is the pace the facility calibrated as sustainable-while-injured, the pace that does not read as flight and does not read as incapacity, the pace that gets you four blocks without anyone calculating what you are. He passes the first block. The rain comes down the same way it came down before the Depot, before the sluice, before the table, indifferent to the debt he just opened and the name still sitting in the room behind him. The second block. The cargo arm drags at the coupling. Silence is still in the borrowed grip, cold blue hamon almost invisible in the rain, the bank still empty because the bank has been empty since the trench and the bank is not the point. *The blade is the point.* He is still holding it. He keeps walking.

Two blocks from the kiosk his mouth opens.

*I will visit you again.* His own voice, his own registers, the cadence slightly long — reading a sentence it has not spoken before. He does not stop walking. Ninety-four steps per minute, exact, the pace stays exact because the pace is the only variable he controls right now and he is going to control it. He counts two steps. Four. Then he asks it flat, his own voice, the question he has been holding since the maintenance lead seated behind his ear eighteen hours ago by the count he is keeping: *What are you called.*

The rain comes down. The pause that follows is not hesitation. It is *rummaging*. Kyle feels it in the back of his skull, behind the auditory contact behind his left ear — a quiet, methodical search through indices the entity does not have, looking for something the entity does not own. First the cybernetic strata: the NeoCortex catalog, the dorsal port row's metadata, the firmware-side fragments the maintenance lead picked up during transfer. The search finds nothing usable. The entity does not have a *name*. The entity has not been called anything in eighteen years because there has been no one to call it anything. It needs a label, and the place it has decided to look for one is *deeper*.

Kyle feels the search cross from cybernetic into organic. It is not painful. It is more invasive than painful. The entity is reading the parts of him that are *meat* — the hippocampal indexing, the long-storage memory tissue, the places his cybernetics do not normally route through and his peers do not know how to access. He feels it sift, polite and patient, the way a librarian sifts a card catalog they have not been given permission to read. Childhood. Iowa. Pre-facility. A county fair when he was six years old, his grandfather's hand on his shoulder, a small wooden booth at the back of the livestock pavilion where a man Kyle never saw worked the strings of two carved figures from below the curtain. He had watched for twenty minutes. He had not understood, at six, that the figures were not alive — and then he had understood, because the man's hand had come up briefly into view to adjust a tangled string, and the strings had become visible, and the magic had not been ruined; the magic had been *named*. The man behind the booth, his grandfather had told him in the walk back to the car, was a *puppeteer*. The word had landed in Kyle the way certain words land in children — load-bearing, archived without filing, carried for forty years against an event that would never come.

The entity finds the word. Kyle feels it find the word. It does not take the word — Kyle still has the memory, the booth, the grandfather, the strings — but it *copies* the word, the way you copy a name out of a contact list, and the entity now has a label.

Then his mouth answers itself: *Puppeteer.*

The cadence is slightly long, the syllables reading a sentence the body has not spoken before — but the word is *his*, in the most specific sense the chapter has produced. He gave the entity the name it just used on him. He gave it forty years ago in the walk back from a county fair he had forgotten he remembered. And then the mouth is his again and he files the name in the same place he filed the salvage glyph and the EMT-spec band model and the specific sound of the cleaver going down twice, and he keeps walking, and the arithmetic resolves in the dry register the NeoCortex reserves for catalog work: the cargo arm is empty hardware. Has been since the junction box on the maintenance landing. The E.L.F. is resident in him — has been since the contact seated, will leave when Puppeteer chooses to leave, will return on Puppeteer's schedule. He has no leverage. He does not stop walking. The AutoDoc kiosk is at the corner of Ashland and Whiting and it is still where it was this morning and that is the only fact he needs right now.

The kiosk reads the necklace. He does not know how. He keyed in with his chin and the panel registered the biometric and then the panel registered something else — the hands at his sternum, the twine, the EMT-spec bands, the tissue window still open — and the AutoDoc opened without requiring him to explain. The surgical arms are the same surgical arms they always are: articulated, precise, indifferent in the specific way of machines that have no stake in what they are repairing. They lift him onto the table with the same gentle math they use on everyone and he lets them. They take the necklace. They take the cargo arm — the coupling releases at the shoulder and the arm goes to the instrument tray and does not move, the status strip dark, shell only — and they slide Silence out of the borrowed grip with the careful, automated reverence machines have for swords and lay it on the side tray and it is there, it is on the tray, it is four feet from his left hand which is about to exist again. The antibiotic pump is already running. The analgesic arrives from the kiosk's own dispensary in a dose large enough to mute the night and he feels it go in and the night begins to mute and as it mutes the NeoCortex feed produces a glyph in the not-factory pattern, the pattern Puppeteer has been signing in, three syllables in old Axiom signage, and Kyle reads it as the anesthesia takes him under: *we are not done.* The AutoDoc's status light goes green. The rain comes down outside the kiosk. Silence is on the side tray. The sentence sits somewhere he cannot easily delete, patient and old, the same frequency as something that has been in the ferrocrete longer than the facility's survey teams were willing to go.

beats.Title: Accusation
beats.Text:
The crocodile does not move. Kyle has been watching it for four minutes — the NeoCortex timestamps involuntarily, a facility habit he never unlearned — and the animal has not moved once, its jaw resting on the heat rock with the particular stillness of something that has learned patience as a survival strategy. He understands that. The tank glass is clean. Someone wipes it daily. That detail costs more than the crocodile.

*The smell is chum and bleach and something underneath both that he is choosing not to identify.*

Hua's hands are the first thing he catalogued when they brought him in, before the chair, before the table, before the long lacquered surface where Silence lay with its friction sheath unbuckled and set beside it like a deed already filed. Real skin. Real nails, cut short and unpainted. The NeoCortex flagged them the same way it flags fire exits and secondary egress points — as a structural anomaly in an environment where chrome is the baseline. In the Gray Zone, unaugmented hands mean poverty or principle. In this room, at this table, they mean neither. They mean she does not need to be faster than anyone in the room, because everyone in the room is afraid of her, which is the only speed that matters.

*His hands are the same category of object for a completely different reason, and she does not know that yet, and he is not going to tell her.*

She stops pacing in front of the tank. The two men at his shoulders have not moved in ninety seconds. The toolkit on the floor between them is a black nylon roll, the kind that fastens with two snaps and opens flat, and Kyle has not looked directly at it because looking at it is information he is not yet prepared to have. Silence is on the table. The angle Hua arranged it — parallel to the table edge, saya toward her, handle toward the room's center — is the arrangement of something already appraised. She has not touched the blade. She has touched the saya twice, with two fingers, the way you confirm a purchase without appearing to need it. Across the table, the chum barrel stands beside the tank, its lid set aside with the same ritual neatness as the friction sheath. The room smells like an argument that was settled before Kyle arrived.

"The Vásquez shipment," Hua says. Not a question. She does not raise her voice. "The Syndicate's contracted route. The Syndicate's contracted fee." She turns from the tank and looks at him with the expression of someone who has already finished a meal and is now simply clearing the table. "You took both."

He says nothing.
