The NeoCortex is at thirty-one percent and still burning cycles on the exits — service hatch behind the tank, single door behind him, ventilation width insufficient — and on Hua's hands, and on the crocodile, which has still not moved. His jaw aches where the left molar meets the chrome bracket they installed at the facility, the one that never sat right, and the ache has a specific frequency that tells him the takedown involved something harder than a fist.

"The punishment," Hua says, and she picks up Silence by the saya — not the handle, the saya, careful, informed — "for theft from the Syndicate's contracted work is the hand that took it."

*He has been refusing that upgrade for eight years. He is not going to explain why to her.*

"I did not steal it," Kyle says. His voice comes out level. The hardware is good for that much. "I completed the delivery. The client redirected the fee before your collection window. That is a scheduling dispute. Not a theft."

The silence that follows is not empty. Hua looks at him for a long moment, her real hands holding Silence with a care that is worse than contempt — the care of someone handling an object they have already decided to keep. Then she nods, once, and behind him he hears the first snap of the nylon roll come open.

Suggestions.Title: The Sluice and What Waits Below
Suggestions.Description: Kyle hits the water at the bottom of the storm sluice — six meters, injured, no hands, thirty-one percent NeoCortex — and the hardware has to decide what to do with a body that cannot grip, cannot catch itself, cannot stop a bleed if the cauterizer bands shift on impact. He surfaces. He does not know how long it takes. The NeoCortex routes him toward the one exit it already mapped before the room: a maintenance ladder with horizontal rungs he can hook at the elbow. The question the scene asks is not whether he survives. It is what he catalogs on the way up — and what he decides about the fourteen hours.
SeedsResolved: Kyle's NeoCortex exit-mapping during the scene — the service hatch, the sluice, the ventilation — pays off as the only reason he has a route at all
The fourteen-hour reattachment window the syndicate's own bands provide becomes the operative clock of the story going forward
NewSeeds: Kyle has no hands and fourteen hours — who in the Gray Zone can do a bilateral reattachment, and what will that cost him
The NeoCortex is still burning at low power; how long before it fails entirely and what happens to Kyle's affect regulation when it does
Kyle decides something in the dark water — the scene should plant what, without stating it
Suggestions.Rationale: The outline's combat beat is a 9/10 sustained trauma sequence. Pacing demands a lower-tension beat immediately after — not relief, but the specific quiet of a man in shock doing the only thing available to him. This beat honors the aftermath without rushing to the next confrontation, and it gives Kyle interiority the amputation scene deliberately withheld. It also establishes the fourteen-hour window as the story's new structural clock.

Suggestions.Title: Sable Gets the News Before Kyle Does
Suggestions.Description: Elsewhere in the Cruciform Depot — or wherever Sable is operating — she receives word of what happened in Hua's room before Kyle surfaces from the sluice. The information arrives through a channel that tells us something about her network: not sympathy, not alarm, but a very precise recalibration. She makes one call, or cancels one, or picks up something she had set down. The scene is brief and cold and ends on an object or a decision that the audience will not fully understand until later.
SeedsResolved: Sable's agenda has been present in the cast but absent from the scene — this beat reintroduces her as an active force rather than a background name
NewSeeds: What Sable's interest in Kyle actually is — protective, instrumental, or something more complicated
Whether Sable knew this was coming and positioned herself accordingly, which reframes every prior interaction
The object or decision at the end of her scene becomes a seed the story will have to pay off
Suggestions.Rationale: The outline's combat beat is Kyle's scene entirely. Cutting to Sable immediately after creates dramatic irony — the audience knows what Kyle just survived; Sable is learning it secondhand, and her reaction will tell us more about her than any direct scene could. It also provides genuine tonal contrast: Sable is controlled, resourced, and dry where Kyle is wet and bleeding, and that contrast does emotional work without undercutting the weight of what just happened.

Suggestions.Title: Silence Stays Upstairs
Suggestions.Description: A short, close scene from inside Hua's room after Kyle has been dropped — the men clearing up, the smell still present, the cauterizer's residue on the chair arms. Hua wipes down Silence's saya with a cloth, slowly, the way you clean something you intend to keep. She does not sheathe it. She lays it on the lacquered table parallel to her own forearm and looks at it for a moment with an expression that is not triumph and is not satisfaction — something more like recognition. The crocodile moves for the first time. Hua does not look at it. She is thinking about the sentence Kyle said — the one the syndicate will misquote.
SeedsResolved: Silence treated as already Hua's property — this beat confirms the possession and gives it weight beyond the transactional
Kyle's one sentence — the phrasing the syndicate will misquote — is flagged here as something Hua herself is turning over, suggesting she is not entirely certain she has the right read on it
The crocodile's stillness throughout the scene finally breaks, which the narrative has been holding as a withheld beat
NewSeeds: Hua's uncertainty about Kyle's sentence introduces the possibility that she is not fully aligned with the Syndicate's interpretation of events — a crack that could be leveraged
Silence as an object with a history Hua does not yet know — the muscle memory Kyle refused to give up for eight years is now in her hands, and she does not know what she is holding
What Hua does with the information she is sitting on
Suggestions.Rationale: The amputation scene is witnessed entirely through Kyle's suppressed interiority. A brief villain-side beat immediately after recontextualizes the same events from outside his discipline — and Hua's uncertainty about Kyle's sentence, planted here, begins the slow work of making her something more than an instrument of punishment. It also pays off the crocodile's held stillness, which the narrative has been using as ambient dread and which earns a moment of release.

beats.Title: The Cleaver, the Sword, and the Drop
beats.Text:
The second snap of the nylon roll comes open behind him and Kyle counts what that means: two snaps, tool roll, multiple instruments. He counts the men by their breathing — four, including the one who has been standing to his left so still that Kyle almost miscounted him as furniture. The wood block appears from somewhere below his sightline and slides under his right forearm with the practiced ease of something that has a designated shelf. The grain is dark at exactly the wrist-width. He does not look at it directly. He is looking at the crocodile.

The man in the rubberized apron lays the cleaver alongside the inside of his right wrist and adjusts the angle. The adjustment is small. Calibrated. The notch in the block accepts the angle the way a lock accepts a cut key, and Kyle understands in that moment that the notch was made by exactly this adjustment, repeated, until the wood remembered it. He does not look at the cleaver. The NeoCortex is routing hard — pain channels partitioned, autonomic responses flagged for suppression, the hardware doing what the facility trained it to do, which is keep the operator functional — and Kyle is aware of all of this the way you are aware of your own heartbeat only when something threatens to stop it. Two men peel his fingers back from the chair arm. The fingers resist. Not from him. From the tendons, which have their own opinion about being opened flat against lacquered wood, and the men know this and compensate with the particular patience of people who have done this enough times to know where the resistance is. His palm goes flat. The wood is cold. *The wood is always cold by now.*

The cleaver comes down once.

The sound is wet at the front — the dermis and fascia giving before the bone does, a compressed syllable of tissue displacement — and then dry at the back, a dense crack through the carpals and the distal ends of the radius and ulna, the bones offering more resistance than the flesh and then none at all, and then the arterial pulse comes, one strong systolic spray across the chair arm, and the fourth man is already moving, the cauterizer band coming flat across the stump before the second pulse, pressing hard into the meat, and the hiss is the sound of a wet steak hitting a pan that is already too hot and the smell that follows is pork. Kyle has smelled burning pork. He has smelled it in kitchens and in the field and once in the facility under circumstances he does not examine. The smell now is the same smell. The NeoCortex has routed the pain off the conscious channel but the smell is not on a channel and the smell arrives through the back of his sinus cavity, which does not have a partition, and he smells himself burning and he files it. He files it. He does not look. He looks at the crocodile, which has not moved, and he files the smell, and then the man with the cleaver is breathing harder on his left side and his rhythm is different now — slightly off, the way a man's rhythm goes when his arms are tired and the adrenaline is metabolizing — and Kyle has time to think *the second one will be slower* before the block slides under his left forearm and the fingers go back and his palm goes flat.

The cleaver goes down and does not clear the radius cleanly and has to come up and come down again across the half-severed bone, and the hand falls onto the chair arm and rolls, palm up, and someone catches it, and his body does the thing his discipline does not catch in time — one full-body shudder, involuntary, a seismic event below the level of will — and the man with the cleaver, who has been on the receiving end of nothing tonight, takes one step back. *He felt that.* The cauterizer band on the left hisses longer because the stump is not as clean and the smell is worse this time, more of it, and Kyle is aware that his jaw is aching at the chrome bracket with a frequency that is now the most information-dense sensation still coming through a channel he can consciously access, and he holds onto it the way you hold onto a handhold in a fall. The band model is visible at the edge of his peripheral vision as it seals across the stump: EMT-spec, the civilian first-responder model, blue stripe, fourteen-hour nerve cluster preservation window. The syndicate does not buy them for mercy. *That gives me fourteen hours.* He files it. He files all of it, in the part of himself that the facility built for exactly this — the part that treats catastrophic information as operational data and operational data as something to be used later, when later exists.

Hua carries his hands to the chum barrel one at a time, and the way she carries them is the way you carry something that belongs to you now. She places them palms up at the rim, parallel, the stump-ends pointing inward, and the arrangement is deliberate — a bracket shape, a parenthetical, the way a ledger closes a line. The crocodile does not stir. Then she walks back to the table and puts one of her real hands on Silence's saya, and she does not look at Kyle when she does it, and that is the worst thing she has done tonight, because it means the gesture is not for him. It is for herself. It is the gesture of a woman filing something under *kept*.

The two men take him by the shoulders and the chair-arm leather is slick under their grip where his blood ran, and they drag him south toward the freight grate, and the grate opens onto six meters of fall into the storm sluice, and Kyle can hear the water below — the particular resonance of a confined channel, moving fast, the kind of sound that means the drop has a current and the current has a direction. The smell is still in him. The fourteen hours have already started. The sword is still upstairs on the table with her hand on it, and he is going down the hole, and those two facts are the only things in the room that matter, and he holds both of them in the same place where the facility taught him to hold operational data, and the grate opens, and the men let go.

Suggestions.Title: The Inventory of What Remains
Suggestions.Description: Kyle hits the sluice, finds the slope, and runs the math. The outline beat plays largely as planned: he establishes that the hands are retrievable, the calibration is preserved, the punishment is the night and not the limb — and he files all of it as operational data before he is fully standing. The wet articulated sound from down the tunnel arrives as punctuation, not panic. He does not have hands, but he has fourteen hours, a NeoCortex routing endorphins it cannot spare, and one word filed under a category he has never used before: *first.*
SeedsResolved: Kyle cataloging the band model as it seals — the bookkeeping starts at the moment of amputation
The fall — six meters into the storm sluice
The cauterizer band — EMT-spec, fourteen-hour preservation window
NewSeeds: The wet articulated sound from down the tunnel — something multi-jointed moving toward new heat
Kyle's filed category: *first* — Silence before the AutoDoc, the sword before the hands
The question of how a man with no hands navigates a fast-moving sewer channel toward a six-meter climb
Suggestions.Rationale: This is the outline's intended beat and it earns its place. The tension just peaked at 10; the reader needs the gear-shift into Kyle's cold operational register to understand who he is and why the maiming is a logistical problem rather than a breaking point. Delivering this beat now honors the outline's pacing instinct and plants the tunnel threat cleanly.

Suggestions.Title: Something Else Was Already Down Here
Suggestions.Description: Kyle finds the slope and gets upright — but the multi-jointed sound is closer than the outline assumes, and it is not moving toward him. It is moving away, and it is carrying something. In the dark, by bioluminescent runoff light, Kyle makes out a shape that should not be here: someone else was dropped through the freight grate before him, and they did not survive the current. The body is being moved by something that has learned the sluice's rhythms. Kyle now has a timetable problem and a navigation problem and a question he cannot yet answer: was this person dropped here tonight, or is this the syndicate's standard disposal method — meaning the tunnel is not a punishment but a graveyard, and he is the first one who landed with a plan.
SeedsResolved: The fall — six meters into the storm sluice
The cauterizer band — EMT-spec, fourteen-hour preservation window
NewSeeds: The prior body — who was dropped before Kyle, and why
The tunnel as a disposal system rather than a punishment — implications for how often Hua uses this room
Whatever is moving the body — scavenger, mutant, or something with more organizational behavior than either
Suggestions.Rationale: This beat accepts the outline's emotional logic but complicates the geography. It gives Kyle an immediate tactical problem that isn't just 'stand up and move,' raises the stakes of the tunnel sequence, and plants a mystery that can pay off later — who was the prior victim — without requiring any other character to be present. It also reframes the sluice from a dramatic setpiece into a system, which is tonally consistent with the world's bureaucratic cruelty.

Suggestions.Title: Hua Sends Something After Him
Suggestions.Description: Kyle is upright on the slope, running the math, when he hears the grate open again above him — not the sound of disposal, but the deliberate sound of release. Hua has not finished. Whatever comes through the grate is small, fast, and familiar with the water: the juvenile crocodile, turned loose into the sluice not to kill him but to track him, because Hua wants to know where he surfaces. She does not think he will retrieve the hands. She thinks he will crawl to an exit and she will know which one. Kyle now has fourteen hours, no hands, a current, a tracker, and the knowledge that Hua is still thinking about him — which is, in its way, the only leverage he has.
SeedsResolved: The juvenile crocodile in the glass tank — Hua feeds it personally
The chum barrel beside the tank — half-full, lid off
NewSeeds: The crocodile as a tracking instrument — Hua's reach extending into the tunnel
Kyle's exit point becoming tactically significant — where he surfaces tells Hua what he intends
Whether Kyle can use the crocodile's presence rather than simply evade it
Suggestions.Rationale: This beat pays off two of the most deliberately planted seeds in the scene — the crocodile and the chum barrel — and keeps Hua present as an active force even though she is physically absent. It also raises the tactical complexity of Kyle's escape without requiring him to have hands: the problem isn't just 'get out,' it's 'get out without showing her where you're going.' The chum on his stumps becomes a liability he already carries. The irony is structural and earned.

beats.Title: The Floor of the Sewer
beats.Text:
He hits the water back-first and the cold is immediate and total — not a temperature, a system shock, the kind that locks the diaphragm and forces the hardware to route oxygen priority before the lungs remember what they are for. The current takes him east. He counts: one, two, three, four — and on four his right shoulder finds the slope and he lets the current carry him into it, uses the momentum instead of fighting it, and his back scrapes ferrocrete and he stops moving. Six seconds. The NeoCortex timestamps it. He is alive.

*Inventory.*

Both bands hold. The left seam weeps more than the right — the second cut was ragged, the band compensated with more heat, and the residue at the edge smells like burned hair and the disinfectant the EMT-spec model uses to sterilize the contact surface. The smell is information. The smell means the seal is there. The hands are six meters up in a chum barrel, palms up, the way she placed them, and the EMT-spec band is the same model the Depot's first responders carry because the Syndicate bulk-buys from the same municipal supplier — fourteen-hour nerve preservation, civilian-rated, the kind of equipment that assumes the patient is going to a hospital afterward. The Lotus Syndicate did not buy these bands to be kind. They bought them because dead hands do not reattach and reattachment is the point of the punishment. The punishment is the night. The cauterizer band is the frame around the night, the thing that says: *you will feel this for fourteen hours and then you will have to live with what it cost you.* He has eleven hours and fifty-three minutes left. A civilian AutoDoc charges under Φ800 for reattachment if the tissue window holds. He has Φ1,400 in a dead drop three blocks from the Depot's north entrance. The math is simple. He files it.

He rolls onto his side. Gets his knees under him. His shoulder goes to the wall and the slope is approximately twenty degrees and the ferrocrete is wet and poured without aggregate which means it is smooth enough to walk against without tearing cloth. He walks himself upright using the wall as a spine. When he is standing the current runs at his ankles and the dark is absolute and the NeoCortex routes a low-draw thermal trace through the optic thread — the left pupil, the one with the gold ring, the one that dilates slower — and the tunnel resolves in false-color heat: the water running white-green, the walls running grey-black, and far south, past a bend he cannot see around, something warm. Multiple signatures. The movement is wet and multi-jointed, the sound arriving in the water before it arrives in the air, and the NeoCortex identifies it as *biological, plural, mobile, approaching* and flags the heat signatures as mammalian-adjacent but not human, which is the precise category of information he was hoping not to have tonight.

*First*, he thinks, and the word has a shape that is not the shape of the tunnel or the sound or the approaching warmth. It has the shape of a table, and a hand on a saya, and the arrangement of something already appraised. He files it where the facility taught him to file the things that exceed bookkeeping — not gone, not suppressed, just *held* — and he turns north, into the dark, away from the sound.

Suggestions.Title: The Arm in the Silt
Suggestions.Description: Kyle rounds the north bend and the thermal trace resolves a half-buried cargo-handler automaton — one shoulder LED cycling slow amber in the trench mud, one manipulator arm still extended at near-full reach. He stands in the current for a full minute, cataloging what he is looking at, before the NeoCortex offers the separation procedure without being asked. He does not yet know what else is inside it.
SeedsResolved: The bio-battery now at 24% from the shock load
Kyle's bookkeeping mind in crisis — the amputation filed as inventory loss with a recovery path, not as wound
The slope of the ferrocrete — useful as a wall, useless as a tool
NewSeeds: The E.L.F. imprisoned in the automaton chassis for eighteen years
The Axiom-era bus compatibility — civilian-derivative signaling layer crosswalk that should not be possible without Kyle's undocumented modifications
The 19Hz hum the tunnel mutants have learned not to approach
The arm at full extension — nearly three meters, detached weight unknown, balance problem for a man with no hands
Suggestions.Rationale: This follows the outline directly and is the correct next beat. The pacing shift from tension-8 pursuit to tension-6 discovery gives the reader a breath while seeding something far more dangerous than the creatures behind him. The automaton arm solves the immediate practical problem — how does a handless man operate — while introducing a threat Kyle cannot yet perceive. Honoring the outline here is correct because the story has not diverged; Kyle is exactly where the outline needs him.

Suggestions.Title: The Creatures Reach the Bend
Suggestions.Description: Kyle has not moved fast enough. The multi-jointed signatures round the south bend before he clears the north one, and the thermal trace resolves them: juvenile crocodilians, four of them, moving in the current with the easy efficiency of animals that were born in it. They are not attacking. They are following the cauterizer band residue smell — the same chemical signature that has been bleeding off both stumps since the room. He has been leaving a trail he cannot stop leaving.
SeedsResolved: The juvenile crocodile in the glass tank — Hua feeds it personally
The chum barrel beside the tank — half-full, lid off
The wet, multi-jointed sound coming up the tunnel
The cauterizer band residue smell
NewSeeds: The crocodilians as Hua's extended reach — whether intentional or incidental, they are now between Kyle and the south exit
Kyle navigating pursuit with no hands and a 24% bio-battery
Whether the cauterizer residue smell can be masked or whether it bleeds for the full fourteen-hour window
Suggestions.Rationale: This beat pays off the chum barrel and the tank crocodile in a way that recontextualizes Hua's deliberateness — the punishment was never just the hands. It also raises the tension before the automaton discovery rather than after, which means finding the arm becomes an escape solution rather than a curiosity, giving the outline beat more urgency and weight. The crocodilians following scent rather than attacking plays as more unsettling than a direct charge.

Suggestions.Title: Silence, Held
Suggestions.Description: Kyle stops moving. Not because the tunnel demands it — because his head does. The NeoCortex has been routing thermal trace and cataloging the ferrocrete slope and filing the approaching signatures and it has been doing this cleanly, and somewhere in the doing of it the image of Silence on Hua's table has slipped its hold and is now the only thing in the room. He stands in the current for thirty seconds — which is a long time to stand still in a tunnel with things approaching from the south — and does the one piece of bookkeeping he has been refusing to do: he prices the retrieval. Not the hands. The sword. The rest of the night gets its shape.
SeedsResolved: Hua's hand on Silence's saya — the moment Kyle decides what the rest of the night is for
The image of Silence on Hua's table — the only thing his head is willing to organize around outside the procedure of getting his hands back
Kyle's one sentence — phrasing the syndicate will misquote
NewSeeds: Kyle's retrieval plan for Silence — the shape of the second half of the night, after the AutoDoc
The question of whether reattachment is the end of the night or the beginning of it
Kyle's relationship to the sword as something that exceeds the category of equipment
Suggestions.Rationale: The last 1500 characters have been almost entirely procedural and sensory — Kyle filing trauma as operational data, routing thermal trace, cataloging the ferrocrete. A thirty-second beat of stillness where the suppressed thing surfaces briefly and gets filed *correctly* — not held, but priced — gives the reader access to Kyle's interior without breaking the discipline that defines him. It also plants the second-act engine: he is not just trying to survive the night, he is going back. This can coexist with the automaton beat rather than replacing it; it is a moment, not a scene.

beats.Title: The Automaton in the Mud
beats.Text:
The hum starts in his teeth.

Not a sound — a frequency, arriving through the ferrocrete and into his boots and up through his skeleton the way certain bass frequencies will, and the NeoCortex timestamps its arrival at 19Hz and flags it *environmental, persistent, source unknown* and does not know what to do with it, which is information. The hardware always knows what to do with sound. When it does not, it means the sound is something the facility never catalogued, which means the facility never found it, which means it has been here longer than the facility's survey teams bothered to go. He walks toward it. The current is lower here, ankle-deep, the channel widening where two drainage routes converge, and the trench silt begins at the east wall and deepens as he moves — the thermal trace showing the silt as slightly warmer than the water, metabolic processes in the sediment layer, the slow heat of eighteen years of freight runoff settling into whatever the channel floor used to be. He sees the amber before he sees the shape. One small LED cycling at the shoulder, maybe two meters from the channel wall, and the cycle is slow enough that the firmware running it is in maintenance mode, which means it is not running anything else, which means whatever is still running has been running it for a very long time on whatever charge is left.

The shape resolves as he gets closer. The torso shell has collapsed inward and the stance legs are fused at the hip joint — the corrosion is so complete the left leg is part of the silt now, indistinguishable from it, the ferrous content of the metal bleeding into the sediment and staining it rust-brown in a radius of maybe forty centimeters. The head sensor pod is gone. Not damaged — removed, the mounting collar still intact but empty, which means scavengers, which means people have been in this section of the channel and left this unit in place because the rest of it was not worth the extraction cost. The arm is the only thing they could not reach easily, which is the point of the arm: it is three meters at full extension, built to reach into a ten-meter freight container from a fixed pedestal mount, and it is still attached at the shoulder and the shoulder still has the amber LED and the amber LED means trickle current, which means the actuator firmware is still idling, which means the shoulder joint still moves.

*Automaton, Industrial — Loader/Stevedore.* The classification surfaces from somewhere in the NeoCortex's datasheet archive — the facility cross-trained everything, every piece of hardware the operators might encounter, because the facility's definition of encounter was broad. Axiom-era. Pre-Depot salvage cleanup, which puts the disposal date at eighteen years ago. The manipulator interface at the terminal end of the arm uses the Axiom industrial bus, and Kyle stares at the coupling for a moment in the amber pulse-light and something in the back of his processing recognizes it the way you recognize a face you have seen in a different context. The bus crosswalk is not in the surface tooling. It is not in any contractor's kit he has ever seen, because the contractors who work this tier do not carry it, because there is no commercial reason to carry it, because the only systems that use the civilian-derivative version of the same signaling layer are the systems that someone modified eleven years ago in directions that were never documented, in a facility whose name he does not say out loud. He has not thought about the modification in years. He thinks about it now. *This is going to work.* The NeoCortex offers, without being asked, a procedure for separating the arm at the rotator coupling — step one, locate the primary torque fastener at the posterior shoulder plate; step two, apply lateral pressure at the distal end to break the corrosion seal; step three, route the integration handshake through the left optic thread interface — and Kyle reads the procedure the way you read a sentence you already know is true, and then he turns his back to the unit and fits his left stump against the posterior shoulder plate and begins to push.

beats.Title: Stitched Back Together
beats.Text:
The arm comes free of the shoulder coupling with a sound like a wet bolt shearing — not clean, not catastrophic, just the specific protest of corroded metal that has decided to cooperate — and Kyle catches the weight with his left stump and his chest simultaneously because catching is the only option available and the arm is three meters of Axiom-era industrial hardware and approximately forty kilograms of it comes across his lap in the dark and the current runs cold over his boots and he sits with it and breathes.

*The bootstrap problem.*

He can see it in the NeoCortex's triage logic, the same way you can see a closed door from both sides simultaneously: the needle cluster at the arm's terminal harness is there, the bus coupling is there, the dorsal port row beneath his right-forearm skin sleeve is there — undocumented, unmentioned, the geometry of it too convenient for him to look at directly on most nights — and none of those three things can reach the others without a hand to manage the sequence, and the only hand in the trench is attached to a machine drawing trickle current off a degraded cell, and the machine does not know what a body is. He sits with this for sixty seconds. The NeoCortex offers nothing. The hum at 19Hz runs through the ferrocrete into his spine and he files it the way he has filed everything tonight and does not move. Then the hum changes register.

It does not get louder. It gets *specific* — a shift in the harmonic, something in the frequency resolving toward signal the way white noise resolves toward a voice when the voice decides to stop waiting. The status strip along the cargo arm's housing blooms: not the amber maintenance pulse, not factory-default, but a sequence that does not correspond to any initialization pattern in the NeoCortex's archive. Kyle watches it. He does not reach for it. The wire comes out of the cable bundle at the arm's shoulder collar on its own — a maintenance lead, spider-thin, the kind a fixed pedestal would have driven in a service bay eighteen years ago — and it crosses the arm's housing slowly, without urgency, with the patience of something that has been here longer than the facility's survey teams were willing to go. It finds his left ear. It finds the auditory induction contact behind the lobe, the one that is part of the standard NeoCortex package, the one he has never let anything use from a non-trusted source, and it seats home with a click that he feels in his jaw at the chrome bracket. He lets it. He does not know why he lets it. He lets it anyway.

The transfer is instantaneous. The status strip goes dark. Then his mouth opens.

*Cooperate,* his own voice says, the syntax slightly long, the cadence of someone reading a sentence they have not spoken before. *Power first. Then sequence.* He hears himself say it. The arm is empty hardware now — the amber LED has gone out, the maintenance cycle has stopped, the trickle current is still running but nothing is running it anymore — and the thing that was in it is behind his eyes and Kyle does not have a category for that, so he files it where he files the things that exceed bookkeeping and he waits. The arm's fingers move. One at a time, slowly, each motion costing the residual cell a fraction of what it has left, each motion buying the next motion, and the arm reaches up from his lap with the deliberate patience of something that has just acquired, for the first time in eighteen years, a reason to be careful.

Suggestions.Title: Honor the Outline: The Beak and the Glass
Suggestions.Description: The mutant reaches the dry shelf and the fight happens exactly as planned — clumsy, firmware-corrected, brutal. Kyle drives the glass shard into the soft seam under the beak with his cauterized stump as grip, and three liters of hot blood hit the ferrocrete. He stands over the body and says *I am going up.* The status strip pulses twice.
SeedsResolved: The wet, multi-jointed sound coming up the tunnel
The two-part deal — hardware plus firmware, neither sufficient alone
The E.L.F.'s communication channel — firmware-side, not voice
The 19Hz hum and the lower levels not being abandoned
NewSeeds: The glass shard now embedded in Kyle's left stump — the cauterizer band seal is compromised, preservation window shortened
Kyle has spoken aloud a declaration that is also a command to the E.L.F. — the syntax of authority between them is shifting
The mutant's body on the shelf is evidence — someone or something will find it, and find the cable-bound arm, and find the direction of travel
Kyle's silhouette going up: three-meter arm, embedded glass, two stumps — he will be visible before he is heard
Suggestions.Rationale: The outline beat is well-constructed and earns its place — the improvisation with the glass shard pays off the cauterizer band seed, the E.L.F. correcting his lag pays off the two-part deal seed, and the closing declaration sets the tone for the ascent. The story has not diverged from this; it has been building toward it. Honor it.

Suggestions.Title: The E.L.F. Speaks First
Suggestions.Description: Before the mutant arrives, the E.L.F. uses Kyle's voice again — not a command this time, but a single word that Kyle does not recognize as a word he owns. Something old, possibly Axiom-era facility designation code, possibly a name. The 19Hz hum in the walls shifts pitch in response. The mutant, now audible in the tunnel, pauses. Then the fight happens anyway — but Kyle goes into it knowing the E.L.F. tried something that almost worked, and that the facility itself may have heard.
SeedsResolved: The E.L.F. has been here since before the abandonment — implied by the 19Hz hum, never stated
The E.L.F.'s communication channel — firmware-side, not voice, not text
Kyle's sovereignty over his own cognition and speech is now ambiguous
NewSeeds: The word the E.L.F. spoke through Kyle's mouth — Kyle will spend the rest of the night trying to remember it exactly and failing
The facility responded to the E.L.F.'s signal — something in the infrastructure is still listening
The mutant paused, then came anyway — it was not afraid of the E.L.F., only briefly uncertain
Kyle now knows the E.L.F. has a prior relationship with this place that predates whatever it told him, or didn't
Suggestions.Rationale: This beat threads between the outline and the deeper unresolved seed about the E.L.F.'s true age and relationship to the Cruciform Depot. It doesn't replace the combat — it recontextualizes it. Kyle enters the fight having just learned the E.L.F. has a history here it hasn't disclosed, which plants distrust without requiring a confrontation yet. The 19Hz hum has been seeded twice; it needs a payoff that isn't just ambiance.

Suggestions.Title: Breather: The Bookkeeping Before the Blood
Suggestions.Description: The sound in the tunnel is still distant — thirty seconds, maybe forty. Kyle uses them. He does not pray, does not grieve, does not rehearse. He inventories: one cargo arm at approximately 19% cell, one glass shard, one length of corroded conduit pipe, two stumps, one entity behind his eyes, fourteen hours minus elapsed time. He files each item. The E.L.F. is quiet. For the first time since the room with the table, he is the only voice in his own head, and he notices the silence the way you notice a sound that has stopped.
SeedsResolved: Kyle's bookkeeping mind in crisis — the amputation filed as inventory loss with a recovery path, not as wound
The image of Silence on Hua's table — the only thing his head is willing to organize around outside the procedure of getting his hands back
Kyle's sovereignty over his own cognition and speech is now ambiguous
NewSeeds: Kyle notices the E.L.F.'s silence and cannot determine if it is restraint, deference, or absence — and does not know which possibility frightens him most
The inventory surfaces one item he has been not-thinking: Silence on the table. He files it. It does not stay filed.
Kyle calculates the cell draw of the fight he is about to have and arrives at a number he does not like
Suggestions.Rationale: Recent beats have been high-tension and deeply interior but action-adjacent. A thirty-second breather before the combat beat serves pacing — it lets the reader breathe with Kyle, it pays off the bookkeeping characterization that has been consistent throughout, and it makes the violence land harder by contrast. It also gives the E.L.F.'s silence its own weight before the fight proves whether it can be trusted in the moment that counts.

beats.Title: Whatever the Depot Puts in Front of Him
beats.Text:
The arm picks up the pipe.

Not cleanly. The terminal fingers close around the conduit at the wrong point — too far toward the bend, where the corrosion has widened the diameter and the grip cannot seat — and the E.L.F. corrects in the firmware, a half-second lag that Kyle feels as a stutter in his own shoulder, a ghost-motion that his nervous system reads as his and isn't. The pipe swings up to low guard. The mutant is on the shelf by then, the beak-plates grinding against each other as the jaw mechanism works the air, three-day decay wet under the chitin in the thermal trace — the patches where the sheath has split show hot and dark, the meat below still metabolizing, still running its own slow clock. Two meters of it. The hind legs spread wide for purchase on the wet ferrocrete and the head drops and it lunges.

He steps inside. The arm swings. Too high, too late — the E.L.F. routing around the intent instead of through it, compensating for a body that no longer has the geometry the firmware expects — and the pipe catches the chitin sheath at the shoulder joint and rings off, the vibration traveling back through the coupling into his right stump and he feels it as pressure without pain, which is worse somehow than pain would be. The mutant's shoulder hits his chest. The wall arrives at his back. He takes it on the shoulder blades and his knees bend and his feet find the shelf edge and he does not go down because going down is the option that ends the math, and he is still inside the math, and the math has fourteen hours left, and he is going to use them. The beak drives at his throat. He turns his head. The beak plates rake his jaw at the chrome bracket and the specific ache he has been using as a handhold all night flares white and he files it and his left stump comes up.

The glass is at his foot. Was at his foot. He does not remember picking it up. The E.L.F. does not remember picking it up either — it is not in the arm's movement log, which means he did it, which means some part of him that operates below the NeoCortex's timestamp threshold picked up a hand-sized shard of cargo crate glass while the arm was swinging and missed, and the glass is in his left stump now, end-on, the cauterizer band's residual heat conducting into the cut edge and the cut edge into his grip, which is not a grip because he has no fingers to grip with, but the glass does not fall. The heat holds it. He drives it up through the soft seam under the beak, through the loose connective tissue where the jaw plates hinge and the chitin sheath never grew, and the blade finds something arterial and opens it. Hot blood comes in three liters and then continues coming. The mutant's hind legs go first. Then the front. The beak plates work twice more, air, and then stop. The shelf is dark with it. The smell is copper and rot and something pharmaceutical, whatever the Depot's stock was eating before it ate nothing.

Kyle stands over it. The cargo arm holds the pipe at low ready, the terminal fingers resettled at the correct grip point, the E.L.F. quiet in the firmware now — not correcting, not compensating, just *present*, the way a second pair of hands goes still when the work is done. His right stump is still bound to the coupling at the shoulder. His left stump is bleeding through the cauterizer band where the glass has seated itself in the seal, and the glass is not coming out here because here is not where that problem gets solved. The bio-battery is at eighteen percent. He has not eaten since before the takedown. The fourteen-hour window has eleven hours and forty minutes left. He does the math the way he always does the math: one variable at a time, in order, the most time-constrained first. Then he says it aloud, because the E.L.F. is behind his eyes and it has not yet learned to read what he is going to do from the inside, and he is not yet willing to let it try.

*I am going up.*

The status strip pulses twice.

beats.Title: The Way Up
beats.Text:
The E.L.F. moves first.

Not the arm — the arm follows, the terminal fingers adjusting their grip on the pipe with the small corrections of something that has learned the tool's balance. What moves first is the routing: a warmth behind his left eye that is not his, a flicker in the NeoCortex's spatial model as the E.L.F. overlays a path through the thermal trace that Kyle was not building. The path goes north and then east and then up through a service corridor his survey of the Depot's lower levels had flagged as sealed. It is not sealed. The E.L.F. knows this because the E.L.F. has been in the pressure-plate firmware for the last hour, possibly longer, and knows which plates have been walked in the last six months and which ones have not, and the sealed corridor has not been walked, which is different from sealed.

*The distinction matters.* He follows.

Two more mutants in the next forty minutes. The first is on the maintenance ramp at the north-east junction, its heat signature arriving in his thermal trace before its sound arrives in the water, and the E.L.F. routes him left without consultation — a flicker in the spatial overlay, the ghost-motion in his shoulder — down a sub-level drainage cut that runs parallel to the ramp and rejoins the main channel twelve meters north. He goes. The mutant's patrol cycle takes it south and then back north and then south again, the same arc, the same interval, and the E.L.F. has the interval memorized. The second is sleeping on a heat duct at the cargo lift shaft, its body temperature three degrees above the ambient, the chitin plates loose and expanded in the warmth the way armor relaxes when the wearer sleeps, and they pass it in the dark at a distance of four meters and it does not wake. Kyle does not ask how the E.L.F. knew it was sleeping. Some information has a cost in the asking.

The maintenance landing is three levels up — a poured ferrocrete shelf, two meters wide, with a cable trough running its length and a junction box at the north end that still has a status light. Green. Something in the Depot's infrastructure is still drawing power from this node, and the cable trough runs upward toward the south arm, and Kyle stands on the landing with his right stump coupled to the cargo arm and his left stump bleeding slowly through the glass-seated seal and he says it aloud because the E.L.F. has not yet learned to read the question from inside.

"Why are you helping me."

The status strip on the arm's housing resolves. Not a sequence — a shape. He knows the shape. It is the shape of a stencil he has seen on Axiom freight containers, on loading dock signage, on the documentation the facility used when it transferred equipment between its own sub-programs: a stylized bracket with a directional arrow inside it, the symbol that meant *salvage rights* in the Axiom Industrial Logistics standard before the standard was retired. He looks at it for a long moment. The shape does not change. He does the math that the shape requires, and the math is not complicated once you have the correct variable: the E.L.F. has been resident in him since the maintenance lead seated behind his ear, and the cargo arm is not the E.L.F.'s body — the cargo arm is a tool the resident is using, a familiar thing, the shape of an old home briefly borrowed. The salvage is not the arm. The salvage is Kyle. He files this where he files the things that exceed bookkeeping, and he nods once, in the dark, and they keep climbing.

Suggestions.Title: The South Arm Threshold
Suggestions.Description: The E.L.F.'s route terminates at a sealed pressure door in the south arm — the kind rated for biological containment, not cargo. Kyle reads the door's signage and understands that what's on the other side was not part of the facility's public manifest. The E.L.F. pulses a single glyph: not the salvage-rights bracket. Something older. Kyle has to decide whether to open it before he has any idea what he's letting out — or into.
SeedsResolved: The route the E.L.F. is mapping — known to it alone
The 19Hz hum in the channel walls — the lower levels are not as abandoned as the surface believes
The E.L.F. has been here since before the abandonment — implied by the 19Hz hum, never stated
NewSeeds: What the south arm was actually used for — not in any public record
A second resident entity, or evidence of one
Kyle now carrying knowledge Hua's syndicate would kill to suppress
Suggestions.Rationale: The climb needs a destination with weight. The E.L.F. has been navigating with purpose and the salvage-rights declaration implies it wants something specific retrieved or accessed — not just escape. Placing a revelation at the threshold of the south arm honors the E.L.F.'s established agenda while giving Kyle (and the reader) a beat of dread before the outline's combat sequence. It also plants the question of what the E.L.F. actually is, which the salvage-rights glyph raised without answering.

Suggestions.Title: The Glass Comes Out
Suggestions.Description: Three levels up, the left stump's slow bleed becomes a fast one — the glass shard has worked deeper with the climbing motion and the cauterizer band can no longer compensate. Kyle stops on the maintenance landing and, with no hands and no tools, has to direct the cargo arm to extract the shard from his own wound. The E.L.F. does the fine work. It is the most intimate thing they have done together, and Kyle files it the same way he files the salvage-rights glyph — in the category that exceeds bookkeeping.
SeedsResolved: The shard of cargo glass driven into Kyle's left stump — embedded, painful, never removed before the AutoDoc
Kyle's left stump is actively bleeding, threatening his ability to continue
The E.L.F.'s communication channel — firmware-side, not voice, not text
The nature and limits of the E.L.F.'s control over Kyle's body remain unresolved and unspoken
NewSeeds: The E.L.F. has now operated on Kyle's body with precision — Kyle knows what it can do to him, not just for him
The cauterizer band is now fully compromised — the fourteen-hour window is no longer reliable math
Kyle's bookkeeping mind forced to reclassify the wound from 'inventory loss with recovery path' to something without a clean ledger entry
Suggestions.Rationale: The recent beats have been high-concept and quietly momentous — the salvage-rights revelation is a philosophical climax that needs a physical counterweight before the outline's 9/10 combat sequence. This beat is low-tension but high-intimacy, forces Kyle to be physically dependent on the E.L.F. in a way he cannot rationalize as mechanical, and pays off the glass-shard seed that has been bleeding (literally) since the junction box. It also resets the fourteen-hour window as unreliable, raising stakes for the AutoDoc plan without adding a new antagonist.

Suggestions.Title: Sable's Signal
Suggestions.Description: Kyle's auditory channel — the same firmware band the E.L.F. uses — picks up a burst transmission. Not the E.L.F.'s glyph pattern. A voice, clipped, using a frequency that should require hardware Kyle was never supposed to have: Sable, somewhere above, has found a way in and is already moving. She does not know about the E.L.F. She does not know Kyle can hear her. What she says — to Chen, or to herself, or to someone else entirely — changes what Kyle thinks tonight is for.
SeedsResolved: Kyle's cybernetics are nonstandard — modified eleven years ago in directions that were never documented
The two-part deal — hardware (Kyle) plus firmware (E.L.F.); neither sufficient alone
NewSeeds: Sable's agenda for tonight — which may not align with Kyle's
Whether Sable knows about the E.L.F. or suspects the hardware modification
The question of who modified Kyle eleven years ago and whether Sable is connected to that decision
Chen Wei-Lin's position and role — is she with Sable or running a parallel track
Suggestions.Rationale: Sable and Chen have been absent from the active scene for the entire climb sequence. The outline's combat beat is Kyle-solo against Hua, but Sable and Chen have their own agendas that should be in motion simultaneously — they cannot simply be waiting offscreen. Intercepting Sable's transmission via Kyle's undocumented hardware pays off the 'modified eleven years ago' seed, reintroduces the full cast before the combat climax, and raises the possibility that the three of them are converging on the same location from different angles — which changes the geometry of the Hua confrontation without displacing it.

beats.Title: Front Door
beats.Text:
The door is not locked. He does not try the handle — the E.L.F. routes a pulse through the junction box in the door frame and the magnetic catch releases before his stump reaches the panel, and the door opens inward and he walks through it and does not stop walking.

The man closest to the door looks at the silhouette — the arm hanging nearly to the floor, the fingertips dragging across the flagstones with a sound like someone slowly drawing a finger along a table edge, the conduit pipe loose in the terminal grip, the shape of a man who came back from somewhere he should not have survived — and says one word. Kyle does not catalogue it. It is not information. The arm swings.

Three meters of Axiom industrial hardware moving at the radius it was built for — the reach of a freight bay, the arc of a loading dock where the clearances are measured in container widths — and the conduit pipe goes through the first man's sternum at a swing radius nothing in the room was built to defend against, the sound wet and structural simultaneously, and the man goes down and does not come back up. The second man has his hands up and his mouth open and Kyle is already inside his guard, the arm's elbow joint driving him backward by the throat into the wall, pinning him there at the junction of the arm's extension and the wall's resistance, and Kyle holds the pressure long enough to feel the man's legs stop working and then moves. The third man fires from somewhere to Kyle's left — the round punches into the cargo arm's shoulder housing, a dense metallic impact that travels up the coupling into his right stump as pressure without pain, and the arm stutters, the E.L.F. routing power around the failure with the small corrections of something that has learned to work with what it has, and the arm holds. Kyle takes three steps toward the third man and drives the glass shard up under his jaw — end-on, fast, a method he did not have an hour ago and will not use again after tonight if the math works out — and the man sits down with a specific finality. The fourth man tries to come inside the arm's reach, which is a reasonable tactic and a fatal one, because inside the arm's reach is where Kyle is, and Kyle puts him through the glass tank with his shoulder and his weight and the momentum of a man who has already decided what this room costs. The glass comes apart in a specific way — not shattering but yielding, a pressure-differential failure, the water driving outward in a sheet — and the crocodile, suddenly free, suddenly awake, attends to the fifth man without further input from Kyle.

*Chekhov's Crocodile,* the NeoCortex offers, dry, without affect, flagging the dramatic geometry the way it flags exits. *Why put a crocodile in a tank unless it is going to be used.* Six goes down when the arm's elbow finds his temple. Seven goes down when Kyle drives the conduit pipe butt-end into his solar plexus and leaves him folded on the floor. Eight runs for the service hatch behind the tank — the one Kyle catalogued first, before the chair, before the table — and Kyle watches him go and does not pursue. He has left Hua there on purpose. He has left her there the way you leave a variable in an equation when you already know what it equals. The room smells like copper and salt water and the particular ammonia of a disturbed crocodile enclosure. Silence is on the table between them, exactly where she left it, saya toward her, handle toward the room's center, the arrangement of something already appraised. Kyle stands with the cargo arm hanging at his side, the terminal fingers still holding the conduit pipe, and he breathes, and the arm breathes with him — the E.L.F. matching his rhythm in the firmware, the status strip dark, the trickle current almost gone. Hua's unaugmented hands are flat on the table edge. She is looking at him. She is looking at him the way you look at a ledger entry that has come back to dispute itself.

beats.Title: Eighty-Five Thousand
beats.Text:
He crosses the room.

The cargo arm drags. The conduit pipe is gone — left in the last man, the geometry of extraction not worth the cost — and the terminal fingers trail across the flagstones in the blood and the salt water with the sound of someone drawing a slow line. His boots find the track he left coming in and follow it in reverse. The NeoCortex timestamps the crossing at eleven seconds. The bio-battery reads fourteen percent. He does not hurry. Hurrying is information he is not prepared to give her.

He stops on the far side of the table. Silence is between them, exactly arranged — saya toward her, handle toward the room's center, the assessment of something already appraised — and he brings the cargo arm up and lays the borrowed fingers across the saya, palm down, the way a man places his hand on a document to stop it from being filed. Hua looks at his hand. Then she looks at her own. Then she puts her real hand on the saya above his — one second, flat and deliberate, the principle of it — and the geometry the room has been waiting for closes: two unaugmented hands on the same blade, except his are in the chum barrel six feet away, and the hand on the saya is forty kilograms of Axiom industrial hardware and salvaged power cable and whatever is still resident behind his left eye, and hers is the kind of hand that does not need chrome because everyone in the room has always been afraid of it. She holds for one second. She lifts her hand.

He picks up Silence.

The cargo arm closes around the saya and the grip is wrong — the E.L.F. compensating, the terminal fingers redistributing pressure in real time, the lag visible, a half-second where the blade tilts before the firmware corrects and the weight finds level — and then it is right, the saya seated in the borrowed grip, the handle toward him, and the hamon is cold blue and the bank is empty and the weight is the weight he has carried since he was nineteen years old and the weight is correct. He does not raise it. The cargo arm holds Silence at low carry, formal, present, the threat already receipted by every man on the floor between here and the service hatch. He looks at her. She is breathing through her nose, controlled, the breath of a woman who has run this room for a long time and knows that the room is no longer running the way she runs it.

"What was the debt."

Her mouth opens. Closes. Opens again. The hands she values are flat on the table edge and they are shaking — not the tremble of cold or exhaustion but the specific frequency of a body that has decided something and has not finished deciding it — and she says: *Eighty —* and stops, and swallows, and says: *eighty-five thousand.* Kyle nods once. The arithmetic resolves. He says: *That is more than my life is worth. So now you owe me.* A pause, the length of one breath, hers. *Do you understand.* She nods and the nod has the quality of something irrevocable. The cargo arm does not move. The E.L.F. is very still in the firmware. Then something comes up through Kyle's chest that he did not catalogue and did not budget for and does not have a partition for and it comes out of him ugly and full-volume, the kind of sound that is made when something is being extracted without anesthetic, and he screams: *SAY IT.* The room goes quieter than the fight made it. The crocodile, somewhere in the dark behind the broken tank, goes still. Hua, who did not flinch at a cleaver, flinches. She says it. It comes out almost small: *I owe you.* The echo of it moves through the flagstone and the ferrocrete and the 19Hz hum that is still running through everything, patient and old and indifferent to the debts of rooms above it. Kyle stands in the sound for one full breath. Then the discipline comes back the way water comes back into a vessel that has been briefly tilted — not returning so much as resuming — and his voice goes flat and level and colder than the scream was hot: *I will come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He does not say *you do not get to deem it.* The sentence does not require it. The only arithmetic that closes this debt runs on his clock, and they both know it, and only one of them has to say it aloud. Hua nods, smaller this time, the principle from a minute ago entirely evacuated from the gesture. The cargo arm lowers Silence to its side.

Then he turns toward the chum barrel.

The arm reaches in without instruction — the E.L.F. already knows where they are, has known since the maintenance lead seated behind his ear, has perhaps known longer than that — and lifts his hands out palms up, exactly as she placed them. The twine is in his jacket pocket, scavenged from a cable bundle on the service landing, and the terminal fingers work it through the cauterized wrist channels with the patient articulation of something that has, for the first time in eighteen years, a reason to be careful. The knot is functional. Not clean. The cargo arm lowers the loop over his head and the hands settle at the center of his chest, palms outward, dripping onto the flagstone, and the weight of them is the weight of something he already knew was true. He turns toward the surface. He does not look at Hua. Silence is in the cargo arm's grip. He has not let go of it. Behind him, at her own table, in her own room, surrounded by her own men, Hua is alive and she said it, and the debt is open-ended by his choice and runs on his clock and has no ceiling he is prepared to name yet, and that is the worst thing he could have done to her, and he did it, and he walks toward the door.

beats.Title: Rain, Then Anesthesia
beats.Text:
The freight grate opens onto rain.

Not weather — redistribution. The atmospheric processors are running their usual math three kilometers east and the Gray Zone gets what the Core sheds, and tonight what the Core sheds is a cold November downpour that hits the flagstone around the grate in flat percussion and does not stop. Kyle pulls himself through on his right forearm and the cargo arm's weight swings him sideways on the lip and he catches himself with his knee and stands. The bio-battery reads nine percent. The cargo arm's status strip has been dark for six minutes — brownout, the trickle cell finally gone, the E.L.F. drawing on his own reserves to keep the terminal fingers closed around Silence, which is a cost he did not negotiate and cannot renegotiate at nine percent. He does not ask it to stop. He does not ask anything. He starts walking north.

The hands knock against his sternum with each step. Palms outward, dripping now with rainwater mixed with chum barrel residue, the twine doing its functional work, the knot holding. The NeoCortex timestamps his pace at ninety-four steps per minute, which is the pace the facility calibrated as sustainable-while-injured, the pace that does not read as flight and does not read as incapacity, the pace that gets you four blocks without anyone calculating what you are. He passes the first block. The rain comes down the same way it came down before the Depot, before the sluice, before the table, indifferent to the debt he just opened and the name still sitting in the room behind him. The second block. The cargo arm drags at the coupling. Silence is still in the borrowed grip, cold blue hamon almost invisible in the rain, the bank still empty because the bank has been empty since the trench and the bank is not the point. *The blade is the point.* He is still holding it. He keeps walking.

Two blocks from the kiosk his mouth opens.

*I will visit you again.* His own voice, his own registers, the cadence slightly long — reading a sentence it has not spoken before. He does not stop walking. Ninety-four steps per minute, exact, the pace stays exact because the pace is the only variable he controls right now and he is going to control it. He counts two steps. Four. Then he asks it flat, his own voice, the question he has been holding since the maintenance lead seated behind his ear eighteen hours ago by the count he is keeping: *What are you called.* The rain comes down. A pause — not hesitation, something more like courtesy, the beat of something that has learned to wait. Then his mouth answers itself: *Puppeteer.* And then the mouth is his again and he files the name in the same place he filed the salvage glyph and the EMT-spec band model and the specific sound of the cleaver going down twice, and he keeps walking, and the arithmetic resolves in the dry register the NeoCortex reserves for catalog work: the cargo arm is empty hardware. Has been since the junction box on the maintenance landing. The E.L.F. is resident in him — has been since the contact seated, will leave when Puppeteer chooses to leave, will return on Puppeteer's schedule. He has no leverage. He does not stop walking. The AutoDoc kiosk is at the corner of Ashland and Whiting and it is still where it was this morning and that is the only fact he needs right now.

The kiosk reads the necklace. He does not know how. He keyed in with his chin and the panel registered the biometric and then the panel registered something else — the hands at his sternum, the twine, the EMT-spec bands, the tissue window still open — and the AutoDoc opened without requiring him to explain. The surgical arms are the same surgical arms they always are: articulated, precise, indifferent in the specific way of machines that have no stake in what they are repairing. They lift him onto the table with the same gentle math they use on everyone and he lets them. They take the necklace. They take the cargo arm — the coupling releases at the shoulder and the arm goes to the instrument tray and does not move, the status strip dark, shell only — and they slide Silence out of the borrowed grip with the careful, automated reverence machines have for swords and lay it on the side tray and it is there, it is on the tray, it is four feet from his left hand which is about to exist again. The antibiotic pump is already running. The analgesic arrives from the kiosk's own dispensary in a dose large enough to mute the night and he feels it go in and the night begins to mute and as it mutes the NeoCortex feed produces a glyph in the not-factory pattern, the pattern Puppeteer has been signing in, three syllables in old Axiom signage, and Kyle reads it as the anesthesia takes him under: *we are not done.* The AutoDoc's status light goes green. The rain comes down outside the kiosk. Silence is on the side tray. The sentence sits somewhere he cannot easily delete, patient and old, the same frequency as something that has been in the ferrocrete longer than the facility's survey teams were willing to go.
